BRECQ: Pushing the Limit of PTQ by Block Reconstruction
entry.content:
Paper / Code

BRECQ is a useful CNN PTQ paper to read before looking at later LLM quantization work. The paper is not only about collecting activation ranges. It frames PTQ as a local reconstruction problem: given a small calibration set, optimize the quantized model so its internal computation stays close to the full-precision model.

The key design choice is the reconstruction unit. Layer-wise reconstruction is too local for modern residual networks. Whole-network reconstruction is too large and easy to overfit when only a small calibration set is available. BRECQ argues that a block is the practical middle point.

Reconstruction Granularity

Figure cropped from the paper PDF: network, stage, block, and layer granularities, together with the corresponding Hessian/Fisher block structure.

The figure explains why the paper prefers block reconstruction. In a residual CNN, a layer does not act alone. Convolutions, nonlinearities, batch norm, and skip connections form a functional block. If PTQ optimizes one layer at a time, it ignores error compensation inside the block.

BRECQ compares four granularities:

Granularity What it optimizes Practical issue
Layer-wise one layer output at a time misses cross-layer dependency
Block-wise one residual/building block balances dependency and overfitting
Stage-wise a group of blocks at the same resolution larger search space and harder calibration
Net-wise final network output overfits easily with limited calibration

The Hessian diagram is the paper’s intuition: layer-wise PTQ keeps only the layer-diagonal part, while full-network reconstruction tries to use the full matrix. Block reconstruction keeps the stronger intra-block interactions and drops weaker inter-block terms.

Optimization Loop

BRECQ optimizes block by block, using calibration inputs, full-precision block outputs, gradients, and optional activation step-size updates.

The procedure is still post-training quantization. Labels are not required, and the model is not trained end to end. For each block, BRECQ records calibration input, the full-precision output, and gradient information. It then optimizes the quantized block output to match the full-precision block output.

At a high level, the objective is:

This is the same practical spirit as AdaRound, but the reconstruction target is a block rather than a single layer. The block gives internal layers room to absorb each other’s quantization errors.

Why Block, Not Layer

The block granularity is the best point in this ablation, especially for MobileNetV2.

The ablation is small but important. With 2-bit weight quantization, block reconstruction beats layer, stage, and net reconstruction on both ResNet-18 and MobileNetV2. The MobileNetV2 gap is especially clear: block reconstruction reaches 59.67, while layer-wise reconstruction reaches 52.13 and net-wise reconstruction collapses to 40.76.

This also explains why “larger reconstruction unit” is not automatically better. Network-wise optimization has the most dependency information, but with only a small calibration set it can fit the calibration examples instead of improving generalization.

Low-bit Results

Weight-only ImageNet results. BRECQ remains usable even at 2-bit weights with 32-bit activations.

For weight-only quantization, BRECQ is much stronger than range-only or layer-only PTQ baselines. On ResNet-18, the 2/32 result is 66.30 compared with 71.08 full precision. On MobileNetV2, 2/32 reaches 59.67 compared with 72.49 full precision, which is a meaningful result for such an aggressive setting.

Fully quantized ImageNet results. Activations are quantized too, which makes the setting much harder.

The fully quantized table is the more deployment-relevant one. At 4/4, BRECQ gives strong results across ResNet, MobileNetV2, RegNet, and MNasNet-style models. At 2/4, most previous PTQ methods fail badly, while BRECQ still produces usable accuracy.

Two details are worth keeping in mind when reading the table:

  • The first and last layers are usually treated more conservatively in low-bit CNN PTQ.
  • The method uses calibration data, but not the full training process required by QAT.

QAT Comparison

BRECQ is a PTQ method, but the paper compares it with QAT-style methods to show the cost/accuracy tradeoff.

The QAT comparison is the deployment argument. For ResNet-18 at 4/4, BRECQ reports 69.60 top-1 with 1024 calibration images and 0.4 GPU hours. QAT baselines use about 1.2M training images and roughly 100 GPU hours in this table.

For MobileNetV2, BRECQ reports 66.57 at 4/4 and 70.74 with mixed precision/8-bit activations. HAQ is still slightly higher in the mixed setting, but at a much higher training/search cost.

Mixed Precision

Mixed precision uses per-layer sensitivity to spend more bits where they matter most.

BRECQ also computes layer sensitivity and uses it for mixed precision. The curve is the useful part: under the same model-size or latency budget, mixed precision sits above uniform precision. That means the method is not only choosing better rounding; it is also learning where low-bit quantization hurts most.

This is the same lesson that later becomes common in deployment work: a single bit-width is easy to implement, but it is rarely the best accuracy-cost point.

Reading Notes

BRECQ’s main idea is modest but durable: choose the reconstruction unit that matches the model’s functional structure. For residual CNNs, that unit is usually a block.

The paper also separates two PTQ questions that are often mixed together:

  • How do we choose quantization parameters for a fixed bit-width?
  • How do we allocate bit-widths under a size or latency budget?

For LLM quantization, BRECQ is not a direct recipe, but it is useful background. GPTQ-style methods target different modules and use different solvers, yet they share the same philosophy: use calibration activations and sensitivity-aware reconstruction instead of minimizing a naive tensor error.

entry.title: BANANAS: Bayesian Optimization with Neural Architectures for NAS
entry.content:
White C, Neiswanger W, Savani Y. BANANAS: Bayesian Optimization with Neural Architectures for Neural Architecture Search. AAAI 2021.

Paper / Code

BANANAS is a predictor-based NAS method. It does not build a differentiable supernet like DARTS, and it does not train a controller like early RL-based NAS. The loop is closer to black-box Bayesian optimization: evaluate a small set of architectures, train a predictor from those observations, use an acquisition function to choose the next candidates, and repeat.

The useful part of this paper is that it does not treat “neural predictor for NAS” as one vague block. It studies five design choices separately:

Component BANANAS choice
Architecture encoding path encoding
Predictor feedforward neural network ensemble
Uncertainty ensemble variance
Acquisition independent Thompson sampling
Acquisition optimization mutation around strong evaluated architectures

The paper is therefore more valuable as an analysis of the BO + neural predictor framework than as a single named algorithm.

BO + Neural Predictor Setup

The search space is a set of architectures. Training an architecture gives its validation error, but this evaluation is expensive. BO tries to spend evaluations where they are likely to improve the best architecture found so far.

The practical loop is:

  1. randomly sample and evaluate several initial architectures;
  2. encode all evaluated architectures;
  3. train an ensemble of neural predictors on architecture/error observations;
  4. generate candidate architectures;
  5. score candidates with an acquisition function;
  6. evaluate the best candidates and update the dataset.

This is attractive because the expensive operation is still actual architecture training, while the predictor is cheap. But the predictor is only useful if the encoding makes architecture similarity visible. That is where path encoding becomes the main idea.

Path Encoding

Most NAS predictors before this paper used an adjacency matrix plus operation labels. That representation is faithful, but it gives the predictor an awkward feature space: node indices are arbitrary, edges are highly dependent, and an edge can be meaningless if it does not belong to an input-output path.

BANANAS instead encodes paths. Each binary feature means that a specific input-to-output operation path exists in the cell.

The left side of the figure is the key intuition. Instead of asking the predictor to infer useful computation from raw adjacency entries, path encoding directly records possible data-flow routes such as:

The full path encoding can be long. On NASBench-101, the paper gives the full length as:

But the right side of the figure is important: truncating the encoding can work well. For NASBench-101, the paper reports that the path encoding can be reduced to about 20 bits without hurting the 150-evaluation BANANAS result. Their explanation is practical: many long or rare paths almost never appear under the random graph sampling procedure, so including them can make the predictor overfit noise.

This is the reusable idea from the paper. The representation is not only smaller than it first looks; it also matches the structure that determines architecture behavior.

Predictor And Uncertainty

BANANAS compares several predictor families on NASBench-101: feedforward networks with adjacency encoding, feedforward networks with path encoding, truncated path encoding, Bayesian neural networks, GCNs, and VAEs.

There are three different measurements in this figure:

Plot What it checks What I read from it
left predictor MAE on held-out architectures path encoding and GCN are the strongest predictors
middle RMSCE calibration error ensembles give better uncertainty estimates than the BNN setup used here
right full BO performance predictor quality must still translate into better search

The right plot matters most. A predictor can have low average error but still rank the best candidates poorly. NAS cares about the top of the ranking, not only global regression quality. In the paper’s full BO setting, the path-encoding feedforward ensemble slightly edges the GCN ensemble, while being simpler and less sensitive to GCN hyperparameters.

The uncertainty story is also pragmatic. The authors use an ensemble of predictors, not because it is theoretically perfect, but because it gives a simple mean and standard deviation for each candidate architecture. That is enough to drive acquisition functions such as expected improvement, UCB, Thompson sampling, and independent Thompson sampling.

BANANAS Pipeline

The final predictor is simple: encode architectures with paths, feed the vectors into an ensemble of feedforward networks, then use the ensemble outputs as performance estimates and uncertainty estimates.

The actual search algorithm adds one more strong engineering choice: do not optimize the acquisition function by sampling candidates uniformly from the whole search space. Generate candidates by mutating architectures that already look good.

The mutation step is doing a lot of work. A neural predictor trained on limited observations is usually more reliable near architectures related to what it has already seen. Mutating good architectures keeps the candidate set in that local neighborhood. This also makes the acquisition function easier to optimize than searching the entire discrete architecture space.

The final BANANAS recipe in the paper is:

Part Choice
predictor input path encoding
predictor model feedforward neural network ensemble
predictor loss MAPE-style loss that emphasizes low validation error
acquisition independent Thompson sampling
candidate generation mutation from the best evaluated architectures

The name sounds broad, but the algorithm is a specific combination of these components.

Results

The main experimental result is on NASBench-101, where the paper can run many controlled trials because architecture accuracies are precomputed. The setup uses about 150 architecture evaluations, reported as 47 TPU hours in the NASBench-101 accounting.

The three panels give useful ablations:

  1. acquisition functions are close, but independent Thompson sampling is a strong default;
  2. mutation beats random, local search, and evolution as the candidate-generation strategy in this setting;
  3. the final BANANAS curve is among the strongest baselines under the same evaluation budget.

The paper also evaluates the DARTS search space. This is less clean than NASBench-101 because it is not a precomputed tabular benchmark, but the comparison is still useful because it checks whether the method can leave a small tabular cell benchmark.

The reported DARTS-space result is:

Method Avg. test error Runtime Note
DARTS, paper 2.76 5 GPU-days gradient-based
DARTS, authors’ rerun 2.68 5 GPU-days same evaluation pipeline
BANANAS 2.64 11.8 GPU-days BO + neural predictor

I would not overread the small difference between 2.68 and 2.64. The more important point is that predictor-based BO remains competitive outside the exact NASBench-101 table, at a cost that is still far below early full-training NAS methods.

Reading Notes

What I would keep from BANANAS:

  • Architecture representation is not a detail. Path encoding changes the predictor’s job from graph interpretation to data-flow feature learning.
  • Predictor accuracy and uncertainty calibration should be checked together. A calibrated but inaccurate predictor is not useful for NAS.
  • Candidate generation matters as much as acquisition scoring. The mutation strategy makes BO practical in a huge discrete search space.
  • Truncating path encodings is not just a memory trick. It can remove rare-path noise and improve predictor behavior.
  • NASBench-style experiments are good for controlled optimizer comparisons, but DARTS-space or real training checks are still needed before treating a method as generally strong.

My main caveat is that BANANAS still relies on a search-space-specific encoding and mutation operator. That is fine for cell-based NAS, but it means the method is not plug-and-play for every architecture family. For a new space, I would first ask: what is the equivalent of an input-output path, and can mutation stay near architectures where the predictor has support?

Overall, BANANAS is a clean paper because it separates the NAS problem into pieces that can be tested: encoding, predictor, uncertainty, acquisition, and candidate generation. The final algorithm works because all five choices are aligned, not because Bayesian optimization alone solves NAS.

entry.title: Big Bird: Transformers for Longer Sequences
BigNAS: Scaling Up Neural Architecture Search with Big Single-Stage Models
entry.content:
Yu J, Jin P, Liu H, et al. BigNAS: Scaling Up Neural Architecture Search with Big Single-Stage Models. ECCV 2020.

Paper

BigNAS is a one-shot NAS paper about making the supernet itself good enough for deployment. The claim is stronger than “use a supernet to rank candidates”: after training one single-stage model on ImageNet, child models from about 200 MFLOPs to 1 GFLOP can be sliced out and used directly, without retraining, finetuning, or other post-processing.

That is the part worth reading carefully. In many weight-sharing NAS methods, inherited accuracy is only a rough ranking signal and the final architecture still needs stand-alone training. BigNAS tries to remove that last step. The paper is therefore less about a new search algorithm and more about a training recipe that makes shared weights behave like a family of pretrained models.

Motivation

The workflow difference is simple:

Traditional one-shot methods train a supernet, search a path, then retrain or finetune the selected child model. OFA-style progressive methods make this more reusable, but still train the elastic model in stages. BigNAS asks whether all child models can be trained simultaneously in one stage and then deployed as-is.

The practical reason is deployment cost. If every target latency, FLOP budget, or device class requires another finetuning or retraining pass, the “cheap” NAS loop still leaves a long tail of engineering work. BigNAS wants the output to be a model family, not just an architecture list.

Search Space

BigNAS uses a MobileNetV2-style MBConv search space. The searchable dimensions are input resolution, channel width, depth, and kernel size; expansion ratio is mostly fixed by the MBConv type in the table.

The important details:

  • Training samples input resolutions from {192, 224, 288, 320}.
  • The supernet contains stage-wise choices for channel count, number of layers, and kernel size.
  • The reported BigNASModels are selected from roughly 200M to 1000M FLOPs, while the single-stage model covers a wider range during training.
  • The paper also notes that after batch-norm calibration, the trained model can generalize to input resolutions not used during training, such as 208, 240, 256, 272, 304, or 336.

This is not a cell-level NAS search space. It is closer to an elastic mobile network family: same backbone grammar, many possible widths/depths/kernels/resolutions.

Single-Stage Training

Sandwich Rule And Inplace Distillation

BigNAS inherits two useful ideas from Once-for-All:

  1. Sandwich rule: in each step, train the largest child, the smallest child, and sampled intermediate children.
  2. Inplace distillation: use the largest child model as the teacher for smaller child models in the same supernet.

This makes sense for the BigNAS goal. The largest child receives normal supervised training, while smaller children learn from a teacher that shares the same weights. The risky part is optimization: small and large child models do not converge at the same speed.

The left plot shows the core dilemma. The big child peaks earlier; the small child keeps improving later. If training stops early, small children are undertrained. If training continues with a decaying learning rate all the way down, the big child can overfit while the small child catches up.

Their fix is deliberately small: exponential decay with a constant ending. Once the learning rate reaches a floor, it stays there until the end. In the main ImageNet setting, the paper uses a 5% floor of the initial learning rate.

The appendix sweep is also useful:

LR floor Smallest model Biggest model Average
3% 76.5 80.8 78.7
5% 76.4 81.1 78.8
8% 76.3 81.3 78.8
10% 76.3 81.3 78.8

The exact floor is not the whole story, but keeping a non-zero ending learning rate is part of making both ends of the supernet usable.

Initialization And Skip Transitions

The paper spends real space on initialization because the single-stage model changes channel counts and fan-in across child models. A fixed-network initialization rule is not enough when the same residual block can be evaluated under many widths.

The BigNAS modification sets the learnable scaling coefficient in the last batch-norm layer of each residual block. This makes the residual branch initially output zeros before the skip connection, so the block starts close to an identity mapping. The paper says this initialization gives around +0.2% in the fixed-network setting, but is much more critical here, with roughly +1.0% improvement in their single-stage setting.

The early-training plot explains why. Naive initialization at the full learning rate can collapse; reducing the learning rate helps but slows training. Modified initialization lets the model keep the original learning rate and still learn quickly.

They also add explicit skip connections at stage transitions. When resolution or channel dimensions differ, the skip path uses 2x2 average pooling and/or 1x1 convolution. This keeps the identity path meaningful even when child models choose different stage configurations.

After the modifications, the small child improves more steadily and the large child avoids the earlier degradation. This figure is more convincing than just reporting the final architecture search result, because it shows the recipe improving the shared-weight training dynamics directly.

Regularization Only On The Full Model

BigNAS also changes where regularization is applied. A naive recipe applies dropout and weight decay to every sampled child model. BigNAS instead applies regularization only when training the largest/full network.

The reason is capacity mismatch. Small child models are already constrained; regularizing them like the largest model can underfit them. In the paper’s ablation, this modified rule improves the small child by about +0.5 top-1 and the big child by about +0.2.

The ImageNet training setup is still heavy: RMSProp, batch size 4096 on TPUs, AutoAugment, Swish, batch-norm post-calibration, weight decay , dropout 0.2 on the full model, and roughly 36 hours of training in the authors’ setup.

Architecture Selection

After training the single-stage model, BigNAS does not run a complicated controller. It uses a coarse-to-fine selection procedure:

First it evaluates coarse skeletons across resolution, depth, width, and kernel choices. Then it picks promising skeletons and mutates them with a finer grid under the target resource budget. The paper uses FLOPs for the reported selection because FLOPs are easier to reproduce than device-specific latency, but it notes that the evaluation metric could also be latency, memory footprint, or predictive accuracy on a target device.

One detail I like: since ImageNet validation is treated as the public “test set” in this community, they use predictive accuracy on the training set for selection after supernet training. That is not a perfect deployment protocol, but it avoids repeatedly tuning on the validation set.

Main Results

The headline result is the Pareto curve and comparison table:

Compactly, the BigNAS family looks like this:

Model Params FLOPs Top-1
BigNASModel-S 4.5M 242M 76.5
BigNASModel-M 5.5M 418M 78.9
BigNASModel-L 6.4M 586M 79.5
BigNASModel-XL 9.5M 1040M 80.9

The comparisons that matter most are compact enough to write directly:

  • Around 200M FLOPs, BigNASModel-S reaches 76.5 top-1 at 242M FLOPs, slightly above Once-for-All finetuned at 76.4 top-1 with 230M FLOPs.
  • Around 400M FLOPs, BigNASModel-M reaches 78.9 top-1 at 418M FLOPs, above EfficientNet-B0 at 77.3 top-1 with 390M FLOPs.
  • Around 600M FLOPs, BigNASModel-L reaches 79.5 top-1 at 586M FLOPs, above EfficientNet-B1 at 79.2 top-1 with 734M FLOPs.
  • Around 1000M FLOPs, BigNASModel-XL reaches 80.9 top-1 at 1040M FLOPs, above EfficientNet-B2 at 80.3 top-1 with 1050M FLOPs.

This table should not be read as a perfectly fair training recipe comparison. The paper itself notes that MNasNet and MobileNetV3 are mainly optimized for on-device latency instead of FLOPs, and different model families use different training hyperparameters. Still, the result is strong for the paper’s central claim: directly sliced child models are competitive without an extra training pass.

Does Finetuning Help?

For me, this is the most important evidence in the paper.

Table 2 tries to finetune selected child models for another 25 epochs with constant learning rates. A too-large finetuning LR hurts badly. A smaller LR mostly changes nothing. For example:

Model Direct slice Finetune LR 0.001 Finetune LR 0.0001
BigNASModel-S 76.5 76.4 76.5
BigNASModel-M 78.9 78.8 78.8
BigNASModel-L 79.5 79.6 79.7
BigNASModel-XL 80.9 80.6 80.8

Table 3 trains the selected architectures from scratch. Even with the better distillation variant, training from scratch remains slightly behind the directly sliced model:

Model Direct slice From scratch From scratch + distill B
BigNASModel-S 76.5 75.3 76.3
BigNASModel-M 78.9 77.4 78.6
BigNASModel-L 79.5 78.2 79.2
BigNASModel-XL 80.9 79.3 80.4

This is the key point. BigNAS is not only saying “our search found good architectures”. It is saying the weight-sharing model has already trained those architectures well enough that the inherited weights beat or match the usual post-processing baselines.

Relation To OFA

BigNAS is close to Once-for-All in spirit: both want one trained network to provide many deployable subnets. The difference is how much staging the training pipeline needs.

Method Training style Deployment claim
Once-for-All Progressive shrinking over elastic dimensions Subnets can be specialized and selected after elastic training
BigNAS Simultaneous single-stage training with a stronger recipe Sliced child models are directly deployable without retraining or finetuning

BigNAS still borrows OFA’s sandwich rule and inplace distillation. The new claim is that progressive shrinking is not strictly necessary if initialization, skip transitions, learning-rate schedule, and regularization are tuned for a very large single-stage model.

Limitations

The result is useful, but it is not a generic proof that all one-shot NAS supernets are deployable.

  • The search space is manually designed around MBConv mobile CNNs. It does not automatically cover arbitrary operators, attention blocks, or hardware-specific kernels.
  • The recipe is expensive: ImageNet-scale supernet training with batch size 4096 on TPUs is still a serious compute budget.
  • The final comparison is mostly FLOP-based. Real deployment often cares about latency, memory bandwidth, activation size, kernel availability, and device-specific scheduling.
  • The method depends on a carefully tuned training recipe. The paper’s strongest message is that supernet training quality matters; it does not make weight sharing automatically reliable.
  • Batch-norm calibration is still needed when slicing and evaluating child models, especially across different input resolutions.

Takeaway

BigNAS is valuable because it changes the question from “which architecture should NAS pick?” to “can a single trained supernet already be the pretrained model family?” The paper’s strongest evidence is Table 2 and Table 3: finetuning and retraining do not meaningfully improve the selected child models.

My main takeaway is that one-shot NAS fails or succeeds mostly at the supernet-training level. Search over a weak shared-weight model is ranking noise; search over a well-trained elastic model can produce deployable subnets directly. BigNAS is one of the cleaner demonstrations of that idea for mobile CNNs.

entry.title: CLIP: Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision
entry.content:
Paper / Code

CLIP is the paper that made “classification by text prompt” feel practical at scale. The idea is simple to state: train an image encoder and a text encoder on internet image-text pairs, then use text descriptions as classifiers at test time.

The important shift is the label space. Instead of predicting one fixed set of dataset labels, CLIP learns a shared embedding space where images and natural-language descriptions can be compared directly. That makes zero-shot classification, retrieval, and open-vocabulary use cases much more natural.

Training And Zero-shot Use

Figure cropped from the paper PDF: CLIP pre-trains with paired image-text examples, then builds a zero-shot classifier from label text.

The training batch contains aligned image-text pairs. The image encoder maps images into a normalized embedding, and the text encoder maps captions into the same embedding space. The model computes all image-text similarities in the batch and uses the matching diagonal as positives.

The zero-shot classifier is just the same mechanism reused at inference time:

  1. Convert each class name into a prompt, such as a photo of a {label}.
  2. Encode all class prompts with the text encoder.
  3. Encode the image with the image encoder.
  4. Choose the prompt embedding with the highest similarity.

That means a new label set does not require training a new linear head. It only requires writing label text.

Why Contrastive Learning

Contrastive training is more data efficient than the caption-prediction baselines in this comparison.

The paper compares three objectives on zero-shot ImageNet accuracy as training compute increases. The contrastive bag-of-words variant learns much faster than the caption-prediction alternatives. The result is not only that more data helps. It is that the objective matters.

The core implementation is short:

The paper’s numpy-like pseudocode: normalized image/text embeddings, scaled cosine similarities, and symmetric cross entropy.

The symmetric loss is worth noting. CLIP trains both image-to-text and text-to-image matching. In a batch of N pairs, each image should match its paired text better than the other N - 1 texts, and each text should match its paired image better than the other N - 1 images.

Prompt Engineering

Prompt engineering and prompt ensembling improve zero-shot classification without retraining the image model.

The paper found that bare class names are often a poor interface to the text encoder. A prompt such as a photo of a {label} gives useful context, and task-specific prompts can help even more. For fine-grained datasets, adding the category type matters, for example writing that the label is a pet, food, aircraft, or satellite image.

Prompt ensembling is the same idea repeated with multiple contexts. Encode several prompts per class, average them in embedding space, and use the result as the text classifier. This costs more text-encoder work when building the classifier, but that cost is amortized across many image predictions.

Zero-shot Evaluation

Zero-shot CLIP versus a fully supervised linear probe on ResNet-50 features across 27 datasets.

CLIP’s zero-shot behavior is uneven, which is one of the more useful parts of the paper. It is strong on datasets where natural language names line up well with visual concepts, such as StanfordCars, Country211, Food101, and Kinetics700. It is weaker on some specialized datasets, including EuroSAT, KITTI Distance, PatchCamelyon, GTSRB, and CLEVRCounts.

This is a good reminder: zero-shot does not mean uniformly strong. It means the model can attempt a task through language. Whether that language interface contains enough signal depends on the dataset.

Few-shot Comparison

Zero-shot CLIP is close to a few-shot linear probe on the same feature space in the paper’s aggregate comparison.

One surprising result is that zero-shot CLIP can match the average performance of a 4-shot logistic regression classifier trained on the same feature space. This does not mean zero-shot is always better than few-shot. It means language priors can be strong enough that a prompt-based classifier is competitive with a tiny labeled set.

The paper also points out a practical research direction: combining the zero-shot classifier as a prior with few-shot learning should be better than treating the two as unrelated methods.

Linear Probe And Model Scale

CLIP features are competitive with strong supervised and self-supervised vision models under linear probing.

The linear-probe results separate two questions:

  • Are the learned visual features good?
  • Is the text-generated zero-shot classifier good?

CLIP is strong on both, but they are not identical. A feature space can be useful while the zero-shot text interface still loses points because the prompt or label set is imperfect. This distinction is important when debugging CLIP-style systems: sometimes the problem is representation quality, and sometimes the problem is the text classifier specification.

Robustness Under Distribution Shift

Zero-shot CLIP reduces the ImageNet robustness gap on several natural distribution shifts.

The robustness result is one of the paper’s most interesting claims. Standard ImageNet-trained models can do well on ImageNet validation but drop sharply under natural distribution shifts. Zero-shot CLIP narrows that gap, likely because it is not tuned directly to the ImageNet training distribution and because its class interface can be adapted with text.

The right side of the figure uses banana examples to make the shift concrete: ImageNet, ImageNetV2, ImageNet-R, ObjectNet, ImageNet Sketch, and ImageNet-A can contain visually different versions of the same semantic class. CLIP handles several of these shifts better than a similarly accurate ImageNet model.

Reading Notes

CLIP’s influence comes from making the text interface a first-class part of visual recognition:

  • Labels become natural-language descriptions.
  • Adding a class can be done by adding text.
  • Retrieval and classification share the same embedding space.
  • Prompt design becomes part of model evaluation.

The limitations are also clear. CLIP learns from noisy web image-text pairs, so biases and spurious correlations matter. It is not a full visual reasoning system. It can fail on fine-grained spatial tasks, abstract synthetic tasks, medical/satellite-style domains, and settings where the class names do not describe the visual decision well.

The practical takeaway for me: CLIP is not “zero-shot magic.” It is a very strong interface between language and visual representations. The quality of that interface depends on pre-training scale, objective design, prompt wording, and whether the target task can actually be expressed through text.

entry.title: ChamNet: Platform-Aware Model Adaptation
entry.content:
Paper / Code

ChamNet is a platform-aware model adaptation paper. It is not mainly about inventing a new operator or cell. It starts from practical building blocks, then reallocates channels, depths, expansion ratios, and input resolution so the resulting model matches a concrete deployment target.

That makes it different from reading a pure NAS paper. The core claim is deployment-oriented: FLOPs are not enough. A model that is good on a mobile CPU may not be good on a DSP, GPU, or server CPU, because each backend has different kernel behavior and memory bottlenecks.

Chameleon Framework

Chameleon separates the main search loop from one-time predictive models for accuracy, latency, and energy.

The framework has two parts:

  • A main search loop using efficient evolutionary search (EES).
  • Predictive models that estimate accuracy, latency, and energy without repeatedly training and measuring every candidate.

The optimization target is straightforward:

ChamNet folds the resource constraint into a fitness score. Candidates that violate the latency or energy budget get penalized, while candidates inside the budget are ranked mostly by predicted accuracy.

This predictor-first design is the paper’s scalability argument. If the accuracy predictor and platform resource predictors are already built, searching for a new use scenario becomes much cheaper than running RL or full hardware-in-the-loop search from scratch.

Accuracy Predictor

The paper compares several accuracy predictors and reports the best leave-one-out MSE from the Gaussian Process regressor.

Only a small number of sampled architectures are fully trained, so the accuracy predictor must work in a low-data regime. ChamNet uses a Gaussian Process regressor because it gives both a prediction and an uncertainty estimate.

The selected samples concentrate near the useful accuracy/FLOPs frontier, while still keeping exploration points.

The sampling rule mixes exploitation and exploration:

  • Exploitation: sample models that look accurate relative to FLOPs.
  • Exploration: sample models where the predictor is uncertain.

This is a practical detail worth remembering. If the predictor only exploits its current belief, it can overfit early mistakes. If it only samples uncertain regions, it wastes training budget. ChamNet deliberately does both.

Platform Metrics

A 1x1 convolution can have very different latency surfaces on different platforms, even when FLOPs look similar.

ChamNet builds an operator latency lookup table from real device measurements. The paper’s latency surface figure is the reason: channel counts create visible discontinuities, and CPU/DSP behavior differs. This is the kind of effect that a FLOPs-only objective misses.

Energy is handled with a predictor too, but it is measured directly from device runs. This makes the framework more expensive to set up than a purely analytical model, but much more relevant for deployment decisions.

Mobile Results

ChamNet-Mobile on Snapdragon 835 CPU.

ChamNet-Mobile on Hexagon v62 DSP.

The mobile experiments adapt MobileNetV2-style inverted residual blocks. The search space includes input resolution, channel count, expansion factor, number of repeated blocks, and stride.

The headline points are:

Platform Constraint ChamNet top-1
Snapdragon 835 CPU 20 ms 73.8
Hexagon v62 DSP 20 ms 75.3
Snapdragon 835 CPU 4 ms 64.2
Hexagon v62 DSP 4 ms 63.6

The tight-latency points are important. At 4 ms, the method still finds a useful architecture instead of only working at comfortable budgets.

Server Results

ChamNet-Res on Intel CPU.

ChamNet-Res on Nvidia GPU.

For server settings, ChamNet adapts ResNet-style building blocks. The paper evaluates Intel Xeon Broadwell CPU and Nvidia GTX 1060 GPU. The curves differ across CPU and GPU, which reinforces the same point as the mobile results: the best architecture family member depends on the platform, not only on the target FLOPs.

Representative reported points:

Platform Constraint ChamNet-Res top-1
Intel CPU 400 ms 78.5
Intel CPU 200 ms 77.2
Nvidia GPU 15 ms 78.6
Nvidia GPU 10 ms 77.7

Energy Results

Energy-constrained ChamNet-Mobile on Snapdragon 835 CPU.

The energy experiment is a good reminder that latency and energy are related but not identical. The paper reports that MobileNetV2 0.75x at 96x96 gets 58.8 top-1 at 19 mJ per run, while an adapted ChamNet model gets 60.0 top-1 at 14 mJ per run. That is a 26% energy reduction while gaining 1.2 percentage points of accuracy.

Comparison And Search Cost

Comparison with manual scaling, RL-based NAS, pruning, and related platform-aware methods.

The table is useful because it mixes accuracy with scaling complexity. RL-based methods such as MnasNet are listed as O(m * n * k), where the factors correspond to models, platforms, and use scenarios. ChamNet separates model accuracy predictors from platform resource predictors and reports O(m + n).

That does not mean ChamNet is free. It still needs a one-time cost for trained architecture samples and platform measurements. The point is that after paying this cost, many platform/budget searches become cheap.

Computation Redistribution

ChamNet shifts compute across stages instead of using a uniform width multiplier.

This is the most concrete design lesson in the paper. The adapted model is not just MobileNetV2 with one global width multiplier. ChamNet moves FLOPs away from some early high-resolution stages and spends more computation later, where it improves the accuracy-latency tradeoff.

The paper reports 71.6 top-1 at 15.0 ms for ChamNet-C, compared with 69.8 top-1 at 16.6 ms for MobileNetV2 0.75x. The method is doing stage-wise allocation, not only shrinking the network.

Reading Notes

ChamNet is strongest as a deployment workflow:

  • Keep proven efficient blocks.
  • Measure the real target platform.
  • Build reusable predictors.
  • Search for stage-wise allocation under the actual budget.

The limitation is also clear. ChamNet depends on the base architecture family and predictor quality. It will not discover a fundamentally new operator class, and it still needs training and profiling samples. But for organizations deploying variants across many devices and budgets, this is a sensible tradeoff: pay the setup cost once, then adapt quickly.

entry.title: Mixture of Experts(MOEs): The Versatile Framework for Scalable AI Solutions
entry.content:
Update

Due to the recent surge in popularity of Mixture of Experts (MOE) in LLMs, this blog was revised on 2024-04-24.

2024-04-24: LLM relevant update

2023-03-28: Summary for Internship in Tencent AI Lab

TensorRT CUDA plugin source code: https://github.com/Baytoro/moe_simple

Motivation

MoE has become so prevalent that it’s now challenging to find a new, large language model (LLM) that isn’t an MoE. Models such as GPT-4, Gemini 1.5, Mixtral 8x7B, and Jamba are all examples of MoE architectures.

The advent of this technology can be attributed to three main aspects:

Sparsity of Neural Networks:

In specific layers, neural networks can become extremely sparse, meaning that the activation frequency of certain neurons is significantly lower than that of others. In other words, not all neurons are utilized every time, which is analogous to the neurons in the human brain.

Many are unaware that neural networks are often excessively large for the majority of the predictions they make.

Take, for example, the task of summarizing an article. The model’s trained parameters not only encompass the data for this capability but also encompass knowledge in physics, mathematics, astronomy, and more. This means that for every prediction, we run the entire network, yet only a small fraction of the model is actually utilized.

Take ChatGPT, for instance. Despite being compelled to run the entire vast network to predict each new word, this demands a significant computational workload. However, for the user’s current question, only a very specific part of the network is activated to assist in predicting the new word.

[1] highlighted the issue of sparse activation in the Transformer model’s Feed-Forward Networks (FFNs). In other words, for a single output, only a small subset of the FFN’s neurons are activated.

In the study, the authors found that after the application of activation functions like ReLU, a majority of the activation values are zero, meaning that only a minority of neurons have non-zero activations, leading to a highly sparse activation pattern in FFNs.

Furthermore, the larger the model, the greater its sparsity. Large models activate a smaller proportion of neurons relative to their total number when processing inputs. For example, in large models, 80% of inputs activate less than 3% of neurons. This phenomenon mirrors the sparse activation patterns observed in the human brain.

In practical use, even with large models, the parameters of their FFNs are not fully utilized, with most neurons corresponding to parameters that remain inactive in the majority of cases.

To address the issue of sparse activation, the paper proposed the MoEfication method, which involves segmenting the FFNs into multiple experts and constructing expert routers to determine which experts to use for each input. This approach enhances the efficiency and performance of the model.

Expertise of Neurons:

The brain is an exceedingly complex organ, composed of various regions, each with its specific area of expertise. Below are examples of some brain regions and the domains of knowledge they excel in:

Frontal Lobes - These are associated with decision-making, planning, problem-solving, personality, and social behavior. Individuals with damage to the frontal lobes may exhibit changes in personality and a decline in decision-making abilities.

Parietal Lobes - Primarily responsible for processing sensory information, such as touch and spatial awareness. Damage to the parietal lobes can lead to an inability to accurately perceive the position or size of objects.

Temporal Lobes - Involved in auditory processing, language comprehension, and memory formation. Damage to the temporal lobes may affect one’s language skills and memory.

For instance, consider a single neuron among the billions in a neural network that may be activated every time an input topic involves “apples,” and yet, this same neuron might also be activated when the input topic involves “telephones.”

One might wonder, what is the connection between the two?

This not only makes neural networks difficult to interpret but is also far from an ideal scenario. A single neuron is expected to be an expert in a variety of topics that are almost entirely unrelated to each other. Imagine being required to be an expert in both neuroscience and geology simultaneously; it would be a daunting task.

As a result, due to the vast scope of knowledge required, these neurons struggle to specialize. What’s worse, the learning curves may conflict with each other, where gaining more knowledge in one subject could impair the neuron’s ability to acquire knowledge in another.

Picture being an expert in mutually exclusive theories, such as materialism and idealism. A significant amount of information from one theory would contradict the other, potentially leading to a collapse in knowledge, rendering you essentially unable to discuss one of the theories coherently.

So, what if we could employ a technique to divide, eliminate, or at least reduce these two issues? This is the problem that the Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) aims to solve.

The MoE approach introduces a modular architecture where a large network is composed of smaller, specialized networks, or “experts,” each responsible for a specific domain of knowledge. By routing inputs to the appropriate expert, the MoE model can focus computational resources and learning efforts on relevant areas, thereby improving interpretability and efficiency.

Limited Computational Resources:

The scale of a model is one of the key factors in enhancing its performance. However, resources are invariably finite at any given stage. Under a constrained computational budget, training a larger model with fewer training steps often yields better results than training a smaller model with more steps.

Workload

Sparse Mixture-of-Experts Layers: These layers are substitutes for the traditional Feed-Forward Networks (FFNs) found in Transformer models. An MoE layer consists of several “experts” (for example, eight experts), with each expert being an independent neural network. In practice, these experts are often FFNs, but they can also be more complex network structures or even MoE layers themselves, creating a hierarchical MoE structure.

Gating Networks or Routing: This component is responsible for determining which tokens are sent to which expert. For instance, in the figure below, the token “More” might be directed to the second expert, while the token “Parameters” could be sent to the first expert. Sometimes, a single token can even be routed to multiple experts. The routing of tokens is a critical aspect of MoE utilization because the router is composed of learned parameters and is pre-trained alongside the rest of the network.

Slow version

Fast version: Sparse to Compact GEMM

By packing tokens assigned to the same expert together, the originally sparse matrix multiplications can be transformed into dense matrix multiplications.

Accelerating Inference (A simple attempt)

This section serves as a summary of my internship at Tencent AI Lab, where my primary focus was on enhancing the inference speed of the Mixture of Experts (MoE) module within Conformer models.

I develop a TensorRT plugin to accelerate Mixture of Experts (MOEs) module by leveraging mixed quantization methods. Token reordering is employed to reduce unnecessary inference in expert networks. And in scenarios with fewer tokens, multi-streaming is also applied to further improve SM occupancy. As a result, we achieve a 25% end- to-end performance improvement on a single NVIDIA T4 with a negligible 0.01% word error rate (WER) increase.

Main code

Step By Step

1. Compute reordered index: gate_idx -> mapping & acc_histogram

2. Mapping copy and quantize

3.1 First Gemm
3.2 Dequantize + BiasSilu + Quantize
3.3 Second Gemm
3.4 Dequantizatize + Bias + ReverseMapping to Output

Limitations

The limitation of the current scenario lies in the fact that it does not take into account the ultra-large-scale matrix multiplication of Large Language Models (LLMs). Therefore, the multi-stream acceleration within a single card cannot meet the acceleration requirements of LLMs. In addition, in the current top-k expert selection, k is only taken as 1. For cases where k is greater than 1, the computational scale and data transfer become more complex, necessitating a more refined consideration.

MOE parallel

  2. Diverse Ensemble Evolution: Curriculum Data-Model Marriage, NeurIPS’18
  3. Diversity and Depth in Per-Example Routing Models, ICLR’21
  4. Adaptive mixtures of local experts, Neural Computation’1991
  5. Outrageously Large Neural Networks: The Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts Layer, ICLR’17

entry.title: End-to-End Object Detection with Transformers
entry.content:
Carion et al. End-to-End Object Detection with Transformers. ECCV 2020.

Paper

DETR is worth reading because it changes the shape of the detection problem. Instead of predicting dense anchors, ranking proposals, and cleaning duplicates with NMS, it predicts a fixed-size set of objects and trains the model with a one-to-one matching loss.

That sounds simple only after the paper exists. The key engineering move is to make “object slots” explicit through learned decoder queries, then force those slots to compete for ground-truth boxes through Hungarian matching.

Motivation

The first figure is the whole paper in one diagram. A CNN extracts image features, a Transformer reasons over them, and a fixed number of predictions is matched against the ground-truth set. A query that does not match any object is trained as the no-object class.

The important contrast with Faster R-CNN style detectors is not just the use of attention. DETR removes several hand-designed detection components:

  • no anchor boxes;
  • no region proposal network;
  • no NMS;
  • no class-specific duplicate suppression heuristic.

The model can do that because the loss itself enforces one prediction per object.

Architecture

The architecture has four parts:

  1. A CNN backbone maps the image to a lower-resolution feature map.
  2. A linear projection converts the CNN channels into the Transformer hidden dimension.
  3. A Transformer encoder adds global context over the flattened feature map, with positional encodings injected because attention is otherwise permutation-invariant.
  4. A Transformer decoder consumes learned object queries and outputs one embedding per query. Each embedding goes through small FFNs for class prediction and normalized box coordinates.

I read the object queries as learned detection slots. They are not proposals with coordinates. They are trainable vectors that ask the decoder to retrieve an object from the encoded image. Since the number of queries is larger than the expected number of objects, unused slots are trained to predict no object.

This design is clean, but it also explains why optimization is harder than in anchor-based detectors. Early in training, a query has no obvious spatial prior. The model must learn both where to attend and how to allocate queries to instances.

Set Prediction Loss

DETR trains on unordered sets. If the ground truth has M objects and the model emits N predictions with N >= M, the target set is padded with no-object entries. The matching step searches for the best permutation:

After this assignment, the Hungarian loss combines classification and box regression:

The box part uses both L1 distance and generalized IoU:

The one-to-one matching is the reason DETR does not need NMS. Two queries can still predict similar boxes, but only one of them receives the object match; the other is pushed toward no-object.

COCO Results

The main COCO table is more nuanced than “Transformer beats detector.” With ResNet-50, DETR reaches the same AP as Faster R-CNN-FPN+:

Method AP AP50 AP75 APS APM APL
Faster R-CNN-FPN+ 42.0 62.1 45.5 26.6 45.4 53.4
DETR 42.0 62.4 44.2 20.5 45.8 61.1
Faster R-CNN-R101-FPN+ 44.0 63.9 47.8 27.2 48.1 56.0
DETR-DC5-R101 44.9 64.7 47.7 23.7 49.5 62.3

The pattern is clear: DETR is strong on large objects and weak on small objects. That matches the architecture. The model reasons globally, but the original feature resolution and attention pattern are not ideal for dense small-instance localization.

Encoder Ablation

The encoder ablation makes the global reasoning argument more concrete. Removing the encoder gives 36.7 AP. Six encoder layers give 40.6 AP, and twelve layers give 41.6 AP. The gain is especially visible on large objects:

Encoder layers AP APS APM APL
0 36.7 16.8 39.6 54.2
3 40.1 18.5 43.8 58.6
6 40.6 19.9 44.3 60.2
12 41.6 19.8 44.9 61.9

This is one of the more useful figures for implementation intuition. The encoder is not a cosmetic Transformer block placed after a CNN. It materially improves scene-level reasoning and query assignment.

Attention And Segmentation

The attention visualization is a good sanity check. Encoder attention follows object boundaries instead of only local texture. That does not prove the model “understands” the scene, but it explains why a global self-attention layer can help with object separation and large-object detection.

The panoptic extension is also important. DETR’s box queries can be reused as instance-level handles: attach mask heads to the decoder outputs, combine them with per-pixel features, and predict segmentation masks. The paper reports competitive panoptic results without changing the core set-prediction idea.

Takeaway

DETR’s contribution is the combination, not any single component:

  • object detection as set prediction;
  • learned object queries as fixed prediction slots;
  • Hungarian matching as the training mechanism that removes duplicate predictions;
  • Transformer encoder-decoder for global assignment and scene reasoning.

The original version also has visible costs. It converges slowly, needs long training schedules, and underperforms on small objects. Later work such as Deformable DETR attacks exactly these points with sparse multi-scale attention and faster convergence. Still, DETR is the clean baseline to understand first because it makes the detector pipeline much less hand-engineered.

entry.title: Direct Federated Neural Architecture Search
entry.content:
He et al. Direct Federated Neural Architecture Search. 2020.

Paper

DFNAS is a practical follow-up to read after FedNAS. FedNAS already asks how to search architectures when data stays on clients. DFNAS asks a more systems-oriented question: can the search be done directly inside the federated training loop, without a separate retraining stage and without DARTS-style multi-path memory cost?

The answer is a DSNAS-like one-path supernet. Each client samples one child network, updates operation weights and architecture parameters locally, and the server averages both.

Motivation

In standard federated learning, the global objective is a weighted sum of local client objectives:

The architecture is usually fixed before training starts. That is a weak assumption in FL:

  • client data can be non-IID, so a manually chosen architecture may fit some clients better than others;
  • the designer often cannot inspect private client data;
  • a second centralized search or retraining stage is expensive and sometimes impossible;
  • DARTS-style continuous relaxation keeps many candidate operations active, which is a bad fit for memory-limited clients.

DFNAS keeps the goal modest: search one global architecture that is ready to deploy after the federated process finishes.

Local Search

For client i, the local objective is written around a sampled structure:

Here Z is the one-hot architecture decision, alpha parameterizes the sampling distribution, and w is the operation weight. A local step roughly does this:

  1. sample a child network Z from p_alpha(Z);
  2. activate only that path in the parent network;
  3. update w with a normal batch gradient;
  4. update alpha with the estimator tied to the sampled architecture probability;
  5. prune weak operations when their architecture weights fall below a threshold.

The memory advantage comes from the one-path execution. If a DARTS cell keeps n candidate operations alive, the forward, backward, and activation memory cost can scale with n. DFNAS trains only one sampled path per step, so the client-side footprint is much closer to training an ordinary child model.

Federated Loop

The server side is FedAvg with one extra object to average. After selected clients finish local search, the server aggregates both weights and architecture parameters:

This is the “direct” part of DFNAS. The searched model is produced by the same communication rounds that train it. There is no proxy dataset, no separate architecture-transfer step, and no final retraining pipeline in the method.

Search Space

The parent network is ShuffleNet-like. That is a good engineering choice for cross-device FL because the candidates are already mobile-friendly. The paper uses:

  • 4 candidates per choice block for cross-silo experiments: ShuffleNet blocks with kernel sizes 3, 5, and 7, plus an Xception block;
  • 3 candidates per choice block for cross-device experiments;
  • a reported 4^20 search space for the cross-silo setting and 3^12 for the cross-device setting.

This is not an open-ended architecture generator. It is a constrained efficient-CNN search space, which makes the one-path federated search realistic.

Communication Curves

The round-accuracy curves are useful because they show a common NAS-in-FL behavior: DFNAS can look bad early while the sampled architecture is still unstable, then catch the fixed baselines after enough rounds.

On non-IID CIFAR-10 with 8 clients and 150 rounds:

Method Final test accuracy
ResNet56 + FedAvg 77.78%
MobileNetV1 + FedAvg 83.41%
DFNAS 88.31%

On non-IID CINIC-10 with 16 clients and 250 rounds:

Method Final test accuracy
ShuffleNetV1 + FedAvg 67.70%
DFNAS 68.35%

The CIFAR-10 gain is the stronger result. CINIC-10 is closer, but still shows that the searched architecture is not just overfitting the small CIFAR setting.

Search Cost

The main comparison with FedNAS is on CIFAR-10 with 8 non-IID clients:

Method Test accuracy Params Total time Search memory
FedNAS 91.43 +/- 0.13% 0.33M 1 GPU day 10,793 MB
DFNAS 92.11 +/- 0.10% 2.1M 0.18 GPU day 1,437 MB

This table should not be read as “DFNAS gives the smallest model.” It does not. The DFNAS model is larger than the FedNAS model in this comparison. The win is search efficiency: much lower memory and much less total search time.

The IID scaling table reports:

Clients Test accuracy Params Total time
2 93.53 +/- 0.10% 2.1M 0.83 GPU day
4 93.31 +/- 0.12% 2.1M 0.43 GPU day
8 92.79 +/- 0.15% 2.1M 0.18 GPU day

Accuracy drops slightly as more clients are used, while wall-clock search time decreases. I would treat this as an implementation scalability result rather than a full proof of robustness under arbitrary heterogeneity.

Takeaway

DFNAS makes architecture search look like normal federated optimization:

  • sample one child model on each client;
  • update weights and architecture parameters locally;
  • average both on the server;
  • derive the final architecture from the learned distribution.

The limitations are also clear. The search space is fixed to efficient CNN blocks, the final model is not always the smallest one, and the method does not add privacy protection beyond ordinary FL. Still, the paper is useful because it attacks the actual bottleneck of federated NAS: client memory and the cost of running search plus retraining as two separate jobs.

entry.title: DeepSeek-V2: Multi-Head Latent Attention and Economical MoE
DistServe: Disaggregated LLM Serving
entry.content:
Zhong et al. DistServe: Disaggregating Prefill and Decoding for Goodput-optimized Large Language Model Serving. 2024.

Paper / Code

DistServe is a systems paper about taking the prefill/decode split seriously. Many LLM serving engines already know that the two phases behave differently, but they still colocate them on the same worker pool. DistServe asks what happens if prefill and decoding are assigned to different GPU groups and optimized with separate parallelism plans.

The paper’s metric is goodput, not raw token throughput. A request only counts if it satisfies both latency constraints.

For LLM serving, the two SLOs are usually time to first token (TTFT) and time per output token (TPOT).

The Interference Problem

Figure 1 is the motivating result. On a 13B model with input length 512 and output length 64, colocated serving reaches about 1.6 requests/s per A100 GPU under a 90% SLO attainment target. If the two phases are measured separately, prefill-only can support about 5.6 requests/s and decode-only about 10 requests/s.

That gap is the opportunity. The shared worker pool is not only under-optimized; it couples two phases with different bottlenecks and different latency targets.

Chunked prefill helps but does not remove the problem. Adding a long prefill job to a decode batch delays decode steps, increasing TPOT. Adding decode jobs to prefill increases prefill execution time, hurting TTFT. The paper’s point is that better batching still leaves a fundamental resource-coupling issue.

Phase Behavior

The two phases stress hardware differently:

Phase Computation shape Main pressure SLO link
Prefill many prompt tokens processed together compute and prompt-length throughput TTFT
Decode one new token per active sequence per step memory bandwidth, KV access, queueing TPOT

Prefill benefits from enough parallelism to reduce first-token latency. Decode benefits from batching many active sequences, but each decode step is small and repeated. A single colocated plan has to compromise between these shapes.

Disaggregation lets the system choose different GPU allocation and model-parallel settings for each phase. The tradeoff is that the KV cache produced by prefill must move to the decode side.

That KV transfer is the main skepticism point for this paper. The architecture only wins when the benefit from eliminating interference is larger than the communication and orchestration overhead.

DistServe Runtime

At runtime, DistServe has a centralized controller. A request is sent to a prefill instance, which computes the first token and KV cache. Then the request is assigned to a decode instance, which fetches the KV cache and continues autoregressive generation.

The implementation details that matter:

  • prefill and decode instances can use different parallelism settings;
  • the placement algorithm accounts for inter-node bandwidth;
  • the controller uses queue lengths to dispatch work;
  • KV cache transfer is pull-based, so decode instances fetch cache when they are ready instead of being flooded by prefill workers;
  • workload profiling can trigger replanning when input length, output length, or arrival rate shifts.

This is more than “put prefill on one GPU and decode on another.” The resource plan is a joint choice over phase split, parallelism, replication, and placement.

End-to-End Results

The chatbot workload uses OPT-13B, OPT-66B, and OPT-175B on ShareGPT. The paper reports that DistServe sustains 2.0x to 4.6x higher request rate than vLLM and 1.6x to 7.4x higher request rate than DeepSpeed-MII under the 90% SLO attainment target.

The second row of the figure varies the SLO scale. DistServe handles 1.8x to 3.2x tighter SLOs than vLLM and 1.7x to 1.8x tighter SLOs than DeepSpeed-MII on the chatbot setting.

The result makes sense: chat has a strong TPOT component. Colocated systems may satisfy TTFT for many requests but fail because decode steps get delayed by prefill interference.

The code completion and summarization tasks stress different sides of the system:

  • Code completion on OPT-66B demands low TTFT. DistServe reports 5.7x higher request rate than vLLM and 1.6x higher than DeepSpeed-MII.
  • Summarization on OPT-66B uses long inputs and a looser TTFT SLO, so TPOT becomes more important. DistServe reports 4.3x higher request rate and 12.6x tighter SLO than vLLM, and 1.8x higher request rate and 2.6x tighter SLO than DeepSpeed-MII.

The same figure also includes the latency breakdown. For OPT-175B on ShareGPT, KV transmission is reported as less than 0.1% of total latency, and over 95% of requests have transfer delay below 30 ms in the testbed. That does not mean transfer is always free, but it supports the paper’s claim that bandwidth-aware placement can keep the cost small.

Ablation And Planner Cost

The ablations separate three ideas:

  1. disaggregate the phases;
  2. choose phase-specific parallelism and resource allocation;
  3. use bandwidth-aware placement.

The paper argues that all three are needed for high goodput. A naive split can still lose if the KV path is bad or if one phase is over-provisioned while the other queues.

The placement algorithm is also designed to be cheap enough for replanning. The paper reports that the largest setting in its evaluation can be solved in under 1.3 minutes, while normal workload shifts happen at a much slower time scale.

What I Would Measure First

Before implementing this design in another serving stack, I would measure four things separately:

Measurement Why it matters
Prefill execution time vs prompt length estimates TTFT pressure and prefill GPU allocation
Decode step time vs active batch size estimates TPOT pressure and decode batching capacity
KV cache size and transfer time decides whether disaggregation overhead is acceptable
SLO attainment under load prevents raw throughput from hiding missed deadlines

If prefill and decode saturate the same resource in the same way, disaggregation is less compelling. If they bottleneck differently, DistServe’s design gives the scheduler more degrees of freedom.

Takeaway

DistServe is the architectural counterpart to continuous batching and chunked prefill. Instead of only improving scheduling inside a colocated worker, it changes the worker layout so prefill and decode can be scaled independently.

The main win is goodput under latency constraints. The main risks are operational: KV transfer, bandwidth-aware placement, failure coupling between phase instances, and workload drift. I read the paper as a strong argument that production LLM serving should evaluate TTFT and TPOT separately before treating a single token/s number as the capacity metric.

entry.title: DrNAS: Dirichlet Neural Architecture Search
entry.content:
Chen, Wang, Cheng, Tang, and Hsieh. DrNAS: Dirichlet Neural Architecture Search. ICLR 2021.

Paper

DrNAS targets the failure mode that makes DARTS-style NAS hard to trust: the search can collapse early into shallow or skip-heavy architectures, and the final cell can be very sensitive to seed, search space, and training length.

The paper’s idea is to treat architecture mixing weights as random variables on the probability simplex. Instead of learning one deterministic softmax vector, DrNAS samples operation weights from a Dirichlet distribution and regularizes that distribution around a stable anchor.

From Softmax Weights To Dirichlet Samples

DARTS relaxes a discrete edge choice into a deterministic mixture:

DrNAS keeps the mixture view but makes the mixing vector stochastic:

The concentration parameter beta controls how samples behave. A broad distribution keeps exploration alive; a concentrated distribution moves toward confident operation selection. The final discrete architecture is derived from the Dirichlet mean.

Figure 1 shows the range of accuracies from sampled architectures on NAS-Bench-201. The solid line is the architecture selected by the Dirichlet mean. This is a useful diagnostic: the method is not only trying to find one good point, but to keep the architecture distribution well behaved during search.

Anchor Regularization

A raw Dirichlet search can still become unstable because the variance of the distribution is hard to control. DrNAS adds an anchor regularizer that keeps the learned concentration parameter near a symmetric Dirichlet anchor:

The paper also connects this regularization to the Hessian of the validation loss with respect to the architecture parameters. The practical reading is simple: DrNAS tries to avoid the sharp, unstable search trajectory that often appears in DARTS.

The gradients still need to pass through samples from a Dirichlet distribution. Since the ordinary reparameterization trick does not directly apply, the paper uses pathwise derivative estimators for Dirichlet samples.

Progressive Learning

DrNAS also introduces a progressive architecture learning scheme:

  • start with a cheaper partial-channel search;
  • gradually increase the channel fraction through network transformation;
  • progressively prune weak candidate operations;
  • keep memory usage controlled while searching on larger tasks.

This is important because a probabilistic search method is not useful if it only works on a tiny proxy cell. The progressive schedule is the bridge from NAS-Bench/CIFAR experiments to ImageNet-scale search.

The discovered normal and reduction cells still look like the usual cell-based NAS artifacts. DrNAS is not replacing the DARTS search space. It is changing the optimization dynamics inside that search space.

CIFAR-10 Results

On CIFAR-10, the paper reports:

Method Test error Params Search cost
DARTS second-order 2.76 +/- 0.09% 3.3M 1.0 GPU day
PC-DARTS 2.57 +/- 0.07% 3.6M 0.1 GPU day
DrNAS without progressive learning 2.54 +/- 0.03% 4.0M 0.4 GPU day
DrNAS 2.46 +/- 0.03% 4.1M 0.6 GPU day

The interesting part is not just the 2.46% number. DrNAS improves while staying in the gradient-based NAS family, which makes the result more comparable to DARTS, PC-DARTS, and SDARTS than to very large RL/evolution searches.

ImageNet Mobile Setting

On ImageNet mobile classification, DrNAS reports 23.7% top-1 error and 7.1% top-5 error with 5.7M parameters and 4.6 GPU days of search. The non-progressive ImageNet version reports 24.2% / 7.3% with 5.2M parameters.

That improvement is small but meaningful in this comparison group. It supports the claim that progressive learning is not only a memory trick; it also improves the final searched architecture.

NAS-Bench-201

NAS-Bench-201 is useful because it reduces the ambiguity of retraining and random search-space quirks. In this table, DrNAS reaches strong accuracy on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet16-120. The reported CIFAR-10 test accuracy is 94.36%, with validation accuracy 91.55%.

I usually trust this kind of benchmark more for stability claims than for absolute model quality. It tests whether the search method consistently selects good architectures inside a controlled finite space.

Regularizer Sensitivity

The anchor regularizer table is a good detail. Without the regularizer, the reported NAS-Bench-201 CIFAR-10 accuracy is 93.78%. A range of regularizer strengths reaches 94.36%, while overly large values fall back to 93.76%.

This suggests the method is not tuned to one exact lambda, but the regularizer is still doing real work. Too little regularization leaves the distribution unstable; too much prevents useful concentration.

Takeaway

DrNAS should be read as a stabilization paper for differentiable NAS:

  • DARTS uses deterministic softmax architecture weights.
  • DrNAS samples architecture weights from a Dirichlet distribution.
  • The anchor regularizer controls the architecture distribution and helps avoid sharp search dynamics.
  • Progressive learning makes the method practical beyond tiny proxy settings.

The limitation is that the search space is still the familiar cell-based NAS space. DrNAS improves how the architecture parameters are optimized; it does not remove the assumptions baked into the candidate operations and cell topology. That is still useful, because instability is one of the main reasons DARTS-style results are hard to reproduce.

entry.title: ELECTRA: Pre-training Text Encoders as Discriminators Rather Than Generators
entry.content:
Paper

ELECTRA is a pre-training paper about signal density. BERT’s masked language modeling objective only predicts a small subset of positions, usually 15% of tokens. The other positions provide context, but they do not directly produce prediction loss.

ELECTRA changes the task. A small generator first replaces some tokens. Then a discriminator reads the corrupted sequence and predicts, for every token position, whether that token is original or replaced. The downstream model is the discriminator, not the generator.

Why MLM Is Wasteful

Figure cropped from the paper PDF: replaced token detection reaches stronger validation accuracy than MLM at the same compute budget.

Masked language modeling is simple and effective, but it spends most of its forward pass on positions that are not prediction targets. If 15% of tokens are masked, the loss is sparse. ELECTRA’s replaced token detection (RTD) objective gives every position a binary classification target.

That does not mean every position is equally informative. Many tokens are easy negatives or easy positives. But the model receives supervision across the full sequence, so the training signal per example is much denser than MLM.

The paper’s compute-efficiency curve is the main motivation. ELECTRA is not proposing a new Transformer encoder architecture. It is changing the pre-training problem so the same kind of encoder can learn more from fewer FLOPs.

Generator And Discriminator

ELECTRA’s pre-training pipeline: a small generator fills masked positions, and the discriminator predicts which tokens were replaced.

The generator is trained with a standard MLM loss. Given an input sequence with some positions masked, it predicts distributions over the original tokens at those masked positions:

$$
\mathcal{L}{\text{MLM}} =
-\mathbb{E}\left[\sum{i \in m} \log p_G(x_i \mid x^{\text{masked}})\right].
$$

Then ELECTRA samples replacements from the generator. The corrupted sequence is fed to the discriminator, which predicts whether each observed token is the true original token:

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\text{RTD}} =
-\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_t
\mathbf{1}(x_t = x_t^{\text{corrupt}})\log D(x^{\text{corrupt}}, t)

  • \mathbf{1}(x_t \ne x_t^{\text{corrupt}})\log(1 - D(x^{\text{corrupt}}, t))
    \right].
    $$

The discriminator is the model kept for downstream tasks. The generator is a training tool.

This makes ELECTRA different from a GAN in the usual unstable minimax sense. The generator is not trained to fool the discriminator through discriminator gradients. It is trained as an MLM, and its sampled outputs create realistic negative examples.

Generator Size

Generator-size and training-algorithm ablations from the paper: a smaller generator is usually the best tradeoff.

The generator must be good enough to create plausible corruptions, but not so large that it wastes compute or makes the task too hard. If the generator is too weak, the discriminator learns shallow cues. If the generator is too strong, the corruption distribution becomes expensive and the replaced tokens can be hard to distinguish.

The paper’s practical answer is to use a generator that is substantially smaller than the discriminator. This gives the discriminator realistic negatives while keeping most of the training compute focused on the model that will actually be fine-tuned later.

There is also a subtle labeling detail. If the generator samples the original token, that position is labeled “original”, not “replaced”. The discriminator is judging the final observed token, not whether the position was selected for masking.

Small-Model Results

Small-model GLUE comparison from the paper PDF: ELECTRA-Small gets strong accuracy with much lower training compute.

Table 1 is the result that makes ELECTRA feel practical. ELECTRA-Small is much cheaper to train than BERT-style baselines and still reaches competitive GLUE performance. This is the strongest evidence for the sample-efficiency claim.

The result is not only about model size. It is about objective efficiency. The discriminator learns from every token position, so the same amount of text can produce more supervised decisions than MLM pre-training.

For resource-constrained encoder pre-training, this is the core takeaway: if the architecture is fixed and compute is limited, changing the pre-training objective can be as important as scaling the model.

Large-Model Results

Large-model GLUE dev and test comparisons from the paper: ELECTRA remains competitive when scaled.

The large-model tables show that ELECTRA is not only a small-model trick. It scales to base and large settings and remains competitive with strong BERT/RoBERTa-style encoders.

The comparison is not perfectly apples-to-apples because large pre-training recipes differ in data, steps, batch size, and tuning tricks. Still, the pattern is consistent: dense RTD supervision gives ELECTRA a strong compute-performance tradeoff.

I read this as a pre-training-objective result rather than an architecture result. ELECTRA keeps the Transformer encoder interface that makes BERT convenient, but changes how the encoder is taught before fine-tuning.

QA Results

SQuAD results from the paper: ELECTRA also transfers to extractive question answering.

SQuAD is useful because it tests token-level span prediction instead of sentence-pair classification. ELECTRA’s gains transfer there too, which suggests the discriminator objective is learning generally useful contextual representations rather than only improving GLUE-style classification.

The key point is that the discriminator must understand whether each token is plausible in context. That is close to the kind of contextual token understanding needed for span extraction.

Compute And Model Scale

Compute-efficiency and model-size ablations from the paper: ELECTRA’s advantage is especially visible for smaller models and limited compute.

The model-size ablation is a good practical warning. ELECTRA’s relative gains are especially attractive in low-compute settings, but the advantage is not a free replacement for scale. As models and training budgets grow, recipe details matter more.

Still, the central idea aged well: do not waste pre-training examples if a denser objective can use them. Many later encoder and generator-discriminator style methods reuse this logic in different forms.

Reading Notes

ELECTRA’s biggest design win is that it removes the train-test mismatch caused by [MASK] tokens. The discriminator sees normal-looking text with replaced words, not a sequence full of artificial mask symbols. Fine-tuning also uses normal text.

The main cost is extra machinery. You need a generator, corruption sampling, and a discriminator loss. The generator/discriminator size ratio becomes a real hyperparameter. But that complexity is modest compared with the compute saved when pre-training encoders under a fixed budget.

My takeaway: ELECTRA is a clean example of improving pre-training by changing where the supervision lands. BERT asks the model to recover a few hidden tokens. ELECTRA asks it to inspect every token and decide whether it belongs. That makes the same text work harder.

entry.title: EAGLE: Speculative Sampling Requires Rethinking Feature Uncertainty
entry.content:
Paper

EAGLE is a speculative decoding paper, but the interesting part is not just “use a smaller model to draft tokens.” Its main claim is more specific: for an autoregressive LLM, the feature right before the LM head is a better draft target than the next token itself.

The target model is still the model being sampled. EAGLE only proposes candidate continuations, and the target LLM verifies them with the usual speculative sampling correction. That matters because speedups are only useful if the decoding distribution is preserved.

Motivation

Figure cropped from the paper PDF: EAGLE improves inference latency on MT-bench across Vicuna and LLaMA2-Chat models under greedy decoding.
