entry.title: [LLM Inference] Sampling and Autoregressive Generate
entry.content:
Reference

  • Teaching repo: Baytoro/LLM_hand
  • Companion notes: docs/12_sampling.md, docs/13_generate.md
  • Runnable scripts: python -m lessons.sampling, python -m lessons.generate
  • Code: tiny_llama/sampling.py, tiny_llama/generation.py

Once the model returns logits, inference still needs a policy for choosing the next token. That policy can be greedy, temperature sampling, top-k sampling, or something more advanced. In this teaching repo I keep it minimal: greedy, temperature, and top-k.

Goal

flowchart LR
    prompt["prompt ids
[B,T]"] --> model["model forward"]
    model --> logits["logits
[B,T,V]"]
    logits --> last["last logits
[B,V]"]
    last --> sample["sample_next_token"]
    sample --> next["next_ids
[B,1]"]
    next --> cat["concat to generated
[B,T+1]"]
    next --> decode["next decode call"]

Generation is not one model call. It is a loop around model calls.

From Logits To Probabilities

For one batch item, logits are arbitrary real scores:

Temperature rescales them:

Then softmax converts scores into probabilities:

The teaching implementation treats temperature = 0 as greedy decoding:

Top-k

Top-k keeps only the largest k logits per batch item:

Shape does not change:

Only the values change; low-ranked tokens become impossible after softmax.

Generate Without Cache

The simplest generate loop feeds the whole generated sequence every time:

This is easy to reason about but wastes work. Every step recomputes the whole prefix.

Generate With Cache

The cache path separates prefill and decode:

The first sampled token is produced from prefill logits. The next model call consumes that sampled token and appends its K/V to cache.

Shape Trace

Step Model input Logits used for sampling Generated shape
prefill [B, T] [B, V] from logits[:, -1, :] [B, T]
sample 1 none yet [B, V] [B, T+1]
decode 1 [B, 1] next loop uses [B, V] [B, T+1]
sample 2 none yet [B, V] [B, T+2]

The ordering is subtle: sampling happens from the previous logits, then the sampled token is fed into the next decode call if another step is needed.

Common Pitfalls

First, generate() returns the prompt plus new tokens. If the prompt length is T and max_new_tokens = N, the output is [B, T + N].

Second, next_ids should stay [B, 1]. Do not squeeze it into [B], because the model expects a sequence dimension.

Third, with cache enabled, do not feed the entire generated sequence after prefill. Feed only next_ids.

Fourth, top-k changes probability support, not tensor shape.

Takeaways

The generation loop is:

Sampling is the policy. KV cache is the mechanism that keeps the loop efficient.

This is the trace I wish I had before reading inference systems papers. It follows one prompt through prefill and then follows generated tokens through decode. The point is not model quality; the point is knowing what shape should exist at every step.

Setup

Use a tiny model:

Symbol Value Meaning
B 1 one prompt
T 2 prompt has two tokens
D 8 hidden size
L 2 two decoder blocks
H 4 query heads
G 2 KV heads
Dh 2 head dimension
V 10 tiny vocabulary

The prompt is:

Timeline

sequenceDiagram
    participant P as Prompt [B,T]
    participant M as Model
    participant C as Cache per layer
    participant S as Sampler

    P->>M: prefill
    M->>C: K/V length T
    M->>S: logits[:, -1, :] [B,V]
    S->>M: next_ids [B,1]
    M->>C: decode, append length +1
    M->>S: logits[:, -1, :] [B,V]
    S->>M: next_ids [B,1]
    M->>C: decode, append length +1

Prefill Trace

Step Tensor Shape
prompt ids input_ids [1, 2]
embedding x [1, 2, 8]
block 0 output x [1, 2, 8]
block 0 cache K/V cache_0.k/v [1, 2, 2, 2]
block 1 output x [1, 2, 8]
block 1 cache K/V cache_1.k/v [1, 2, 2, 2]
final logits logits [1, 2, 10]
next logits logits[:, -1, :] [1, 10]

The cache sequence length is 2 because the prompt had two tokens.

First Decode Step

Assume the first sampled token is:

The model consumes only that token:

Step Tensor Shape
decode input next_ids [1, 1]
token embedding x [1, 1, 8]
new q q [1, 1, 4, 2]
new k/v before transpose k/v [1, 1, 2, 2]
new k/v in cache layout new_k/new_v [1, 2, 1, 2]
cache after append cache.k/v [1, 2, 3, 2]

block output x [1, 1, 8]
logits logits [1, 1, 10]

The score shape [1, 4, 1, 3] is the decode signature: one query token attends to three cached key positions.

Second Decode Step

The next decode token again has shape [1, 1], but the cache is longer:

Step Shape
decode input [1, 1]
old cache [1, 2, 3, 2]
new k/v [1, 2, 1, 2]
new cache [1, 2, 4, 2]
attention scores [1, 4, 1, 4]
logits [1, 1, 10]

Only the last axis of scores grows as the sequence grows.

Debug Checklist

When I debug a cache path, I check these invariants:

Invariant Expected
decode input rank always [B, 1]
cache list length num_layers
cache head count G, not H
cache append dimension dim=2
RoPE start position old cache.seq_len
decode score shape [B, H, 1, T_total]
decode logits shape [B, 1, V]

This is almost the whole generate algorithm. The rest is validation and sampling options.

The entire KV-cache inference path can be summarized as:

entry.title: [LLM Inference] What This Tiny Llama Leaves Out
entry.content:
Reference

  • Teaching repo: Baytoro/LLM_hand
  • Full review note: docs/feishu/llm_forward_inference_review.md
  • LLaMA paper: LLaMA: Open and Efficient Foundation Language Models
  • Llama 2 paper: Llama 2: Open Foundation and Fine-Tuned Chat Models
  • Llama 3 paper: The Llama 3 Herd of Models

This final post is a boundary marker. The tiny implementation in this series is useful because it is small enough to inspect. But real Llama inference is not just these 200 lines of model code. It adds tokenizer details, checkpoint loading, optimized kernels, paged memory, batching, scheduling, and system-level tradeoffs.

What The Tiny Model Teaches Well

The tiny model is good for the core forward path:

flowchart LR
    ids["token ids"] --> emb["embedding"]
    emb --> norm1["RMSNorm"]
    norm1 --> attn["RoPE + GQA attention"]
    attn --> res1["residual"]
    res1 --> norm2["RMSNorm"]
    norm2 --> mlp["SwiGLU MLP"]
    mlp --> res2["residual"]
    res2 --> head["LM Head"]
    head --> logits["next-token logits"]

It teaches these invariants:

Concept Shape to remember
token ids [B, T]
hidden states [B, T, D]
q [B, T, H, Dh]
k/v in GQA [B, T, G, Dh]
K/V cache [B, G, T_cache, Dh]
logits [B, T, V]
next-token logits [B, V]

These are the shapes I want in muscle memory before reading optimized inference code.

What It Leaves Out

Real Tokenization

The teaching tokenizer is a greedy toy tokenizer. Real Llama models use trained subword tokenizers with special tokens, chat templates, BOS/EOS handling, and compatibility constraints between tokenizer files and model checkpoints.

Real Weights

The tiny model initializes random weights. It demonstrates dataflow, not language quality. Loading real weights introduces:

Issue Why it matters
parameter naming checkpoint keys must match module names
tensor parallel layout weights may be sharded
dtype fp16/bf16/fp8/int4 affect kernels
tied embeddings some models tie embedding and LM Head weights

Optimized Attention Kernels

The teaching code uses explicit q @ k.transpose(...) and softmax. Production inference often uses FlashAttention-like kernels or decode-specialized kernels. Those kernels preserve the same mathematical contract but avoid materializing some intermediate tensors.

The learning version exposes:

An optimized kernel may never store that full tensor. The shape reasoning still helps, but the memory behavior changes.

Paged KV Cache

The teaching cache is a simple concatenated tensor:

Serving systems often use paged or block-based KV memory so many requests can share GPU memory efficiently. The logical shape remains similar, but physical storage becomes an indirection problem.

Batching And Scheduling

The tiny generate loop assumes a simple batch. Real serving systems handle:

Serving issue Example
mixed prompt lengths different T per request
continuous batching new requests join while others decode
prefill/decode imbalance prefill is compute-heavy, decode is memory-heavy
cancellation user stops generation
streaming tokens are returned before the full sequence finishes

This is where systems papers become necessary.

How I Would Continue

After this series, the natural next topics are:

  1. PagedAttention and block-based KV memory.
  2. FlashAttention and decode attention kernels.
  3. Continuous batching and request scheduling.
  4. Tensor parallel inference.
  5. Quantized weight-only inference.
  6. Speculative decoding.

Those are not replacements for the shape-first model. They are layers on top of it.

Series Index

# Post
1 A Shape-First Map of Llama Forward
2 Token IDs, Embedding, and LM Head
3 RMSNorm and QKV Projection
4 RoPE: Position Enters Query and Key
5 Causal Self-Attention by Shapes
6 GQA and MQA: Fewer KV Heads
7 KV Cache: Prefill and Decode
8 SwiGLU MLP and the Transformer Block
9 Assembling a Decoder-Only Model
10 Sampling and Autoregressive Generate
11 A Token-by-Token KV Cache Trace
12 What This Tiny Llama Leaves Out

Takeaways

The tiny repo is not an inference framework. It is a map. It makes the core forward path small enough to hold in working memory:

Once that map is stable, the larger serving stack becomes a series of implementation choices rather than a black box.
