entry.title: LQ-Nets: Learned Low-Bit Quantization
entry.content:
Paper: LQ-Nets: Learned Quantization for Highly Accurate and Compact Deep Neural Networks

LQ-Nets is useful because it asks a basic question: why should the quantization levels be fixed before training? Uniform quantization is easy to implement, but the distribution of weights and activations may not be uniform. LQ-Nets learns the quantizer itself.

Motivation

Binary and ternary networks save a lot of memory, but their codebooks are extremely restrictive. Uniform multi-bit quantization is more expressive, but it still assumes that equally spaced values are a good fit. LQ-Nets keeps the low-bit representation but learns the basis values used to reconstruct quantized tensors.

The figure shows that activation and weight distributions are not always well matched by a naive uniform grid. The learned basis gives the quantized model more freedom at the same bit-width.

Methodology

The quantized value is represented as a linear combination of learned basis values. Conceptually, for a scalar or tensor element:

where contains learned basis values and is a low-bit encoding vector. Instead of selecting from a fixed grid such as , the model learns the set of reconstruction values.

The optimization alternates between two coupled tasks:

  1. update the network weights under quantized forward propagation;
  2. update the quantization basis so the low-bit representation better matches the learned tensor distributions.

This is more flexible than LSQ-style step-size learning because the codebook is not forced to be a scaled uniform grid. The cost is deployment complexity: arbitrary learned levels are less friendly to standard integer GEMM kernels.

Results

The paper reports low-bit CNN results on CIFAR and ImageNet. Learned quantization improves over fixed binary/ternary and uniform quantization baselines, especially when bit-width is very small. The benefit comes from using the same number of bits more effectively rather than increasing model capacity.

Takeaway

LQ-Nets is a learned-codebook baseline. It is not the most hardware-friendly endpoint, but it explains why quantization levels matter. Later papers make different tradeoffs:

  • LSQ learns only the step size, keeping a uniform grid.
  • SqueezeLLM uses non-uniform quantization for LLM weights, but with serving cost in mind.
  • NF4 in QLoRA chooses a data type matched to normally distributed pretrained weights.

The common idea is that the quantizer is part of the model design space.

Learned Codebook Versus Learned Scale

LQ-Nets learns more than LSQ. LSQ keeps the levels uniformly spaced and learns the spacing. LQ-Nets learns basis values, so the spacing itself can become non-uniform.

This gives better accuracy at very low bit-width, but it changes the hardware story. A uniform quantizer can often be implemented as integer multiply-accumulate plus scale. A learned codebook may require lookup/decode logic or specialized kernels. That is why learned-codebook papers often look strong in accuracy tables but need a separate deployment analysis.

A useful comparison:

Method Learned quantity Hardware friendliness
PACT activation clipping threshold high
LSQ uniform step size high
LQ-Nets quantization basis/codebook lower, unless kernel supports it

What The Paper Contributes

The paper’s real contribution is showing that the quantizer has trainable capacity. Once the model is forced into 2-bit or 3-bit weights/activations, the choice of levels can matter as much as the choice of architecture. This idea later reappears in NF4 and SqueezeLLM, where the quantization levels are chosen to fit actual weight distributions rather than a generic uniform grid.

Source-Level Notes

LQ-Nets learns the quantization levels instead of fixing them to uniform bins. A quantized value is represented by a small number of binary bases:

The basis vector determines the actual quantization levels. Given assignments, the basis can be solved by least squares; given the basis, the assignments are updated by projection. This alternating structure is the main difference from LSQ, where the quantization grid stays uniform and only the step size is learned.

What The Learned Codebook Buys

Uniform quantization is hardware friendly, but it assumes values are evenly worth representing across the range. Learned quantization can put levels where the layer actually needs them. That helps especially at very low bit widths, where every level matters.

The cost is implementation complexity. A learned non-uniform codebook is not the same as a plain integer GEMM path. If the target is a real accelerator, the codebook must either be converted into an efficient lookup/decode path or restricted enough to map to hardware. This is why LSQ-style learned scale became more widely used in QAT baselines, while LQ-Nets remains useful as a conceptual learned-quantizer reference.

Experiment Reading

The result tables should be read with the hardware question in mind. Learned quantization levels can recover accuracy at 1-2 bits, but they create a less regular numeric format. If the final kernel must decode arbitrary codebook entries before multiplication, the practical speedup may be smaller than the bit width suggests.

The paper is strongest as evidence that quantization levels are model parameters. This contrasts with post-training min/max calibration, where the grid is determined by tensor statistics. In LQ-Nets, the grid itself is optimized for the task.

A reproduction should compare three variants: fixed uniform levels, learned scale with uniform levels, and learned non-uniform levels. That isolates whether the gain comes from learning the range or from learning the shape of the codebook.

entry.title: Transformers are SSMs: Generalized Models and Efficient Algorithms Through Structured State Space Duality
Medusa: Simple LLM Inference Acceleration Framework with Multiple Decoding Heads
entry.content:
Cai T, Li Y, Geng Z, et al. Medusa: Simple LLM Inference Acceleration Framework with Multiple Decoding Heads.

Paper

Medusa accelerates LLM decoding by adding multiple prediction heads to the original model. Instead of using a separate draft model, it predicts several future-token candidates from the target model’s hidden states and verifies them efficiently.

Architecture

The figure shows the base model with additional Medusa heads. Each head predicts tokens at a future position. The heads are lightweight compared with a separate draft LLM.

Why Not A Separate Draft Model

Classic speculative decoding uses a small draft model and a large target model. That requires maintaining two models and matching their token distributions. Medusa attaches draft heads directly to the target model, which simplifies deployment.

Tree Verification

Medusa does not verify only one draft chain. It builds a tree of candidate continuations and uses tree attention to verify multiple branches in one target-model forward pass.

The key metrics are:

Metric Meaning
acceptance length average number of accepted tokens per target forward
head accuracy how often draft tokens match target choices
distribution preservation whether generated text follows the original model distribution

Medusa-1 And Medusa-2

Medusa-1 trains only the additional heads and keeps the backbone frozen. Medusa-2 fine-tunes more of the model for better head quality. The deployment tradeoff is training cost vs acceptance rate.

Limitation

The upper bound is head quality. If the heads propose poor candidates, tree verification wastes target forward passes. This connects Medusa to later work such as EAGLE and multi-token prediction, which also try to produce better draft tokens.

Takeaway

Medusa is appealing because it is simple: add heads, draft a tree, verify with the target model. The method is most useful when the added heads produce high acceptance rates without changing the output distribution.

entry.title: MnasNet: Platform-Aware Neural Architecture Search for Mobile
Mooncake: KVCache-Centric LLM Serving
entry.content:
Paper: Mooncake: A KVCache-centric Disaggregated Architecture for LLM Serving

Mooncake is valuable because it reads like a production systems paper. The design is organized around KV cache: where it is produced, stored, reused, moved, and evicted.

Motivation

Long-context serving changes the cost model. A request may spend a large amount of time and memory in prefill, then reuse or transfer a huge KV state during decode. Treating KV cache as temporary scratch memory is no longer enough.

The figure shows Mooncake’s disaggregated architecture. Prefill, decode, and KV-cache management are separated into components that can be scheduled independently.

Methodology

Mooncake is KV-cache centric in three senses:

  1. Placement. The system decides where KV cache should live across workers.
  2. Transfer. Prefill-generated KV must be moved efficiently to decode resources.
  3. Reuse and overload behavior. Long-context workloads benefit from managing cache lifetime explicitly.

Compared with DistServe, Mooncake emphasizes production traffic and long context. The system is less about one theoretical split and more about operating the split under real workload pressure.

Results

The paper reports improvements for Moonshot/Kimi-like serving workloads. The benefits come from better KV placement and disaggregated resource management rather than a single faster kernel.

Takeaway

Mooncake pushes the PagedAttention lesson to the cluster level. KV cache is a large data object. For long-context LLMs, serving architecture should be designed around KV movement and lifetime, not only model weight placement.

Production Angle

Mooncake matters because real long-context traffic is not a clean benchmark. Requests may have huge prompts, repeated context, overloaded queues, and uneven decode lengths. A production system must decide not only how to execute a request, but where to keep the KV state and when to move it.

KV Cache As Data

The paper treats KV cache like a data object with lifecycle:

  1. created by prefill;
  2. transferred or placed for decode;
  3. possibly reused;
  4. evicted under pressure.

This is different from viewing KV cache as temporary tensors inside one GPU process.

Relation To PagedAttention

PagedAttention solves memory layout inside a worker. Mooncake asks cluster-level questions around KV movement and disaggregation. Both are necessary for long-context serving; they operate at different layers of the stack.

Source-Level Notes

Mooncake takes the disaggregation idea into a KV-cache-centric production design. Long-context workloads make KV cache the dominant state object. The model weights are static, but KV cache is request-specific, large, and constantly moving through the system.

The paper’s architecture should be read around this question: where should KV cache live so that prefill, decode, reuse, and overload handling remain efficient?

Production Reading

The interesting part is that KV cache becomes data, not a temporary tensor. Once contexts are long and prefix reuse matters, the serving system needs placement, transfer, eviction, and reuse policies for KV cache.

This is a different layer from PagedAttention. PagedAttention manages KV memory inside a GPU worker. Mooncake reasons about KV cache across a disaggregated service. The same object moves from kernel memory layout to cluster-level scheduling policy.

Experiment Reading

Mooncake is most convincing under long-context and overloaded scenarios. Short prompts with little prefix reuse do not stress KV-cache management enough to show the architecture’s value. The paper should be read with production traffic in mind: uneven prompt lengths, repeated prefixes, and changing load.

The KV-centric view also changes what metrics matter. GPU compute utilization is not enough. KV transfer volume, cache hit rate, cache eviction behavior, and SLO satisfaction become first-class metrics.

A useful comparison is DistServe. DistServe separates phases for goodput. Mooncake adds a stronger claim that KV cache placement and reuse should organize the system. That is a production architecture argument, not only a scheduling heuristic.

Reproduction Checklist

A useful reproduction should generate traffic with long prompts, repeated prefixes, and overload periods. Then report TTFT, TPOT, goodput, KV-cache hit rate, and KV transfer volume. Average latency alone is too weak for this paper.

I would also separate prefill cache creation from decode cache consumption. Mooncake’s architecture is built around moving and reusing KV cache as a first-class object, so the metrics should show where that object is stored, reused, evicted, and transferred.

Boundary / Failure Mode

The limitation is operational complexity. Once KV cache is a distributed object, failures, migration, eviction, and load balancing all affect correctness and latency. The paper is valuable because production long-context serving needs that machinery, but it is not the first system I would build for a small single-node deployment. The architecture pays off when KV cache dominates service behavior.

entry.title: Neural Architecture Optimization
entry.content:
Luo R, Tian F, Qin T, et al. Neural Architecture Optimization. NeurIPS 2018.

Paper

NAO frames NAS as representation learning plus continuous optimization. Instead of searching directly in a discrete architecture space, it trains an encoder, a performance predictor, and a decoder. Architectures are mapped into a continuous latent space, moved toward higher predicted performance, then decoded back into discrete architectures.

This is an interesting alternative to RL, evolution, and differentiable supernets. It tries to make discrete architecture search look like gradient-based optimization in a learned space.

Encoder-Predictor-Decoder

The pipeline is:

  1. encode architecture (x) into latent vector (e_x);
  2. predict performance (f(e_x));
  3. update the latent vector by ascending predictor gradient;
  4. decode the improved vector into a new architecture.

The latent update can be written as:

The figure shows the continuous architecture manifold and the encoder-decoder loop. The method depends heavily on whether this latent space is smooth enough to support meaningful gradient steps.

Why This Is Useful

NAO separates architecture representation from architecture evaluation. If the encoder learns useful structural semantics, nearby points in latent space should decode to similar architectures with similar performance.

That gives the predictor gradient a chance to be meaningful. If the latent space is not smooth, the update becomes an artifact of the predictor.

Failure Modes

There are three major risks:

  • the predictor may rank architectures poorly;
  • the decoder may produce invalid or low-quality architectures after latent updates;
  • the latent step may leave the training distribution.

For this reason, predictor ranking correlation and decoder reconstruction accuracy are more informative than a single final accuracy number.

Relation To Later Work

NAO is connected to predictor-based NAS and generative architecture search. The general idea is still useful: learn an architecture embedding, then search in that embedding space.

Takeaway

NAO is not the final form of deployment NAS, but it is conceptually valuable. It shows that architecture search can be treated as continuous optimization if the architecture representation is learned carefully enough.

entry.title: Better & Faster Large Language Models via Multi-Token Prediction
NAS-Bench-101: Towards Reproducible Neural Architecture Search
entry.content:
Ying C, Klein A, Christiansen E, et al. NAS-Bench-101: Towards Reproducible Neural Architecture Search. ICML 2019.

Paper

NAS-Bench-101 is a benchmark paper, not a method paper. Its contribution is to make NAS experiments repeatable. Instead of requiring every researcher to retrain thousands of architectures, it tabulates a large set of cell architectures with fixed training and evaluation results.

This changes NAS research from “I spent more GPU days” to “under the same query budget, which optimizer finds better architectures?”

Search Space

The search space is a directed acyclic graph cell with a fixed maximum number of nodes and edges. Intermediate nodes choose operations such as convolution and pooling. Equivalent graphs are canonicalized to reduce duplicates.

The figure shows the outer CNN skeleton and example cell structures. The benchmark focuses on small cell DAGs, not complete mobile or Transformer architectures.

What Is Stored

For each valid architecture, NAS-Bench-101 stores training results under a fixed recipe. This allows algorithms to query validation accuracy without actually training the model.

The most useful evaluation is a best-so-far curve under a fixed number of queries. Reporting only the final best architecture hides sample efficiency.

Query Protocol

A serious benchmark use should specify:

  • query budget;
  • whether validation or test accuracy is used for search;
  • number of random seeds;
  • whether intermediate learning-curve information is allowed;
  • whether the final architecture is retrained outside the benchmark.

If an optimizer can query indefinitely, the benchmark becomes a lookup table.

Limitations

NAS-Bench-101 is intentionally constrained. It does not cover latency, large-resolution ImageNet training, mobile inverted residual blocks, or Transformer dimensions. Winning on NAS-Bench-101 proves something about a small DAG cell space, not universal architecture design.

Takeaway

NAS-Bench-101 made NAS algorithm comparison much more scientific. It is best used as a controlled diagnostic environment. If a method is unstable even here, it is unlikely to be reliable in a real deployment search space.

entry.title: NAS-Bench-201: Extending the Scope of Reproducible Neural Architecture Search
entry.content:
Dong X, Yang Y. NAS-Bench-201: Extending the Scope of Reproducible Neural Architecture Search. ICLR 2020.

Paper

NAS-Bench-201 is a compact, fully enumerated NAS benchmark. It was designed to make algorithm comparison cheaper and more reliable than repeated GPU-heavy search experiments.

Search Space

The cell has four nodes. Each edge chooses one operation from a fixed operation set, including zero, skip connection, convolution, and average pooling.

The figure shows the macro skeleton and the operation choices inside the cell. The space is small enough to enumerate, but rich enough to expose common NAS failure modes.

What Is Stored

For each architecture, the benchmark stores results on several datasets, including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet16-120. This enables cross-dataset ranking analysis.

That is a major advantage over single-dataset benchmarks. A method that only works on one dataset may be exploiting dataset-specific quirks.

Why It Matters

NAS-Bench-201 is useful for diagnosing search behavior:

  • Does the optimizer beat random search under the same query budget?
  • Does it collapse toward skip connections?
  • Is the ranking stable across seeds?
  • Does performance transfer across datasets?

These questions are hard to answer when each architecture requires a new training run.

Limitations

The benchmark is still a small image-classification cell space. It does not include device latency, mobile inverted residual blocks, segmentation, detection, or Transformer architectures.

Therefore, success on NAS-Bench-201 should be treated as algorithm sanity evidence, not proof of deployment superiority.

Takeaway

NAS-Bench-201 is one of the most useful controlled testbeds for NAS. If a method is unstable here, it is probably not ready for larger and noisier search spaces.

entry.title: NAS-Bench-301 and the Case for Surrogate NAS Benchmarks
entry.content:
Siems J, Zimmer L, Zela A, et al. NAS-Bench-301 and the Case for Surrogate Benchmarks for Neural Architecture Search.

Paper

NAS-Bench-301 addresses a limitation of tabular NAS benchmarks. Fully enumerating a small search space is useful, but realistic spaces such as DARTS are too large to tabulate exhaustively. NAS-Bench-301 trains surrogate models to predict architecture performance in a larger space.

Why Surrogates

NAS-Bench-101 and NAS-Bench-201 are deterministic lookup tables. That is excellent for reproducibility, but their spaces are small. A surrogate benchmark trades exactness for scale.

The figure compares optimizer behavior on the true benchmark and surrogate models. The key question is whether the surrogate preserves rankings and search trajectories well enough for algorithm comparison.

Benchmark Pipeline

The pipeline is:

  1. sample many architectures from a DARTS-like space;
  2. train and evaluate them with a fixed recipe;
  3. fit surrogate predictors, such as graph neural networks or gradient-boosted trees;
  4. use the surrogate as a cheap performance oracle.

This makes it possible to run many NAS optimizers under controlled query budgets.

Surrogate Risk

The main risk is surrogate exploitation. A search algorithm can find architectures that the surrogate predicts to be strong but that would not train well in reality.

Therefore, a strong use of NAS-Bench-301 should include:

  • held-out surrogate error;
  • ranking correlation such as Kendall tau;
  • best-so-far trajectories;
  • a small number of real retraining checks for final candidates.

What It Solves

NAS-Bench-301 makes large-space optimizer comparison more practical. It is especially useful for studying optimizer behavior: random search, evolution, Bayesian optimization, DARTS variants, and predictor-guided methods.

Takeaway

NAS-Bench-301 is a bridge between exact tabular benchmarks and expensive real search. It is not a final oracle, but it makes large search-space experimentation much more reproducible.

entry.title: NAS-BERT: Task-Agnostic and Adaptive-Size BERT Compression with Neural Architecture Search
entry.content:
Xu J, Tan X, Luo R, et al. NAS-BERT: Task-Agnostic and Adaptive-Size BERT Compression with Neural Architecture Search.

Paper

NAS-BERT applies NAS to BERT compression through a task-agnostic supernet. The goal is to amortize the large pretraining cost and then select smaller BERT-style architectures for downstream tasks and deployment constraints.

Search Space

The search space includes hidden size, number of attention heads, FFN width, and operation choices. This is more flexible than simply dropping layers from BERT.

The figure shows candidate operation sets and separable convolution structure. NAS-BERT explores compressed encoder architectures rather than only scaling the original Transformer block.

Supernet Training

The expensive part is task-agnostic supernet pretraining. Once trained, the supernet can support many downstream architecture choices.

This cost amortization is the core engineering idea. If each task required a full pretraining search, the method would be much less attractive.

Model Selection

For each deployment target, a subnet is selected and fine-tuned or distilled. The selected model can trade accuracy for latency or parameter count.

The cost accounting should include:

Cost Meaning
supernet pretraining large one-time cost
architecture search selecting a subnet
downstream adaptation fine-tuning or distillation

Relation To AdaBERT

AdaBERT is more task-specific. NAS-BERT is more amortized and task-agnostic. Both show that NAS can be useful for compression when the search space includes width, head count, FFN size, and operation type.

Takeaway

NAS-BERT is a model-family compression paper. Its value is not just a smaller BERT, but a reusable supernet that can produce adaptive-size encoder models under different constraints.

entry.title: Learning Transferable Architectures for Scalable Image Recognition
entry.content:
Paper

NASNet is the paper that turns the expensive NAS-RL idea into a more transferable design pattern. Instead of searching a whole ImageNet-scale network directly, it searches for small convolutional cells on CIFAR-10, then stacks those cells to build larger ImageNet models.

The important contribution is the search space. Once the cell is found, the number of cell repeats and filter counts can be scaled without changing the cell topology.

Motivation

The original NAS-RL paper could discover good architectures, but searching directly over a large full network is expensive. NASNet asks a more reusable question:

Can we search for a small building block on CIFAR-10 and transfer that block to ImageNet?

The answer depends on constraining the search space. If the controller searches arbitrary whole networks, transfer is fragile. If it searches repeated motifs, the learned component can be reused at different depths, resolutions, and compute budgets.

Contribution

The paper contributes:

  1. The NASNet search space: architectures are built from repeated Normal Cells and Reduction Cells.
  2. A transfer recipe: search the cell on CIFAR-10, then stack it for ImageNet.
  3. ScheduledDropPath, where the probability of dropping a path increases during training.
  4. Strong results on CIFAR-10, ImageNet classification, and COCO detection with NASNet features.

The headline numbers:

Task Result
CIFAR-10 2.40% error
ImageNet 82.7% top-1 / 96.2% top-5
ImageNet mobile-scale setting 74.0% top-1
COCO detection 43.1% mAP test-dev

Methodology

Normal and reduction cells

NASNet fixes the macro layout and searches the repeated cell structure. There are two cell types:

  • Normal Cell: keeps the feature map resolution.
  • Reduction Cell: reduces spatial resolution by using stride-2 operations.

For CIFAR-10, cells are stacked between a few reduction points. For ImageNet, the image is larger, so the network uses more reduction stages. The topology of each cell is learned; the number of repeats and initial filters are scaling knobs.

Controller block

Each cell is built from blocks. In the paper’s main NASNet-A search, . For each block, the controller predicts five decisions:

  1. Select the first hidden state.
  2. Select the second hidden state.
  3. Select an operation for the first hidden state.
  4. Select an operation for the second hidden state.
  5. Select how to combine the two outputs.

The operation set includes identity, pooling, standard convolution, factorized convolution, dilated convolution, and depthwise-separable convolution. At the end of the cell, unused hidden states are concatenated to form the output.

NASNet-A cell

The found NASNet-A cells contain many separable convolutions and learned skip-style connections. There are no manually inserted residual links between cells; the searched cell already learns its own internal connectivity.

ScheduledDropPath

The authors found ordinary DropPath was not enough. ScheduledDropPath drops paths in a cell with a probability that increases linearly over training. This is a small but practical detail: without strong regularization, these searched cells can overfit.

Results

CIFAR-10

Model Params Error
NAS v3 + more filters 37.4M 3.65%
NASNet-A (6 @ 768) 3.3M 3.41%
NASNet-A (6 @ 768) + cutout 3.3M 2.65%
NASNet-A (7 @ 2304) + cutout 27.6M 2.40%
NASNet-C (4 @ 640) 3.1M 3.59%

The large NASNet-A with cutout reaches 2.40% error averaged across 5 runs, and the best single run reported in the paper is 2.19%.

ImageNet transfer

The key claim is transfer: the cells are searched on CIFAR-10, then all ImageNet models are trained from scratch with those cells.

Model Params Mult-Adds Top-1
Inception ResNet V2 55.8M 13.2B 80.1
NASNet-A (7 @ 1920) 22.6M 4.93B 80.8
SENet 145.8M 42.3B 82.7
NASNet-A (6 @ 4032) 88.9M 23.8B 82.7

NASNet-A reaches 82.7% top-1 and 96.2% top-5 on ImageNet with fewer mult-adds than SENet in the comparison table.

Smaller compute setting

For the <1.5B mult-add regime, the paper reports:

Model Params Mult-Adds Top-1
MobileNet-224 4.2M 569M 70.6
ShuffleNet (2x) ~5M 524M 70.9
NASNet-A (4 @ 1056) 5.3M 564M 74.0

This is one reason NASNet mattered: the same cell family could scale down and still beat mobile-oriented baselines from that period.

Detection transfer

The paper also plugs NASNet-A ImageNet features into Faster R-CNN on COCO. The best reported test-dev mAP is 43.1%, which supports the claim that the learned features transfer beyond classification.

Takeaway

NASNet’s main lesson is that the search space can matter more than the controller. By forcing architectures to be made of reusable cells, the paper makes search results transferable across scale.

There are still limitations. The search is expensive, and the method assumes a hand-designed macro skeleton with normal/reduction cell placement. But the cell-based formulation became the template for many later NAS papers because it turns an architecture into something you can scale, compare, and reuse.

entry.title: NATS-Bench: Benchmarking NAS Algorithms for Architecture Topology and Size
entry.content:
Dong X, Liu L, Musial K, Gabrys B. NATS-Bench: Benchmarking NAS Algorithms for Architecture Topology and Size. TPAMI 2021.

Paper

NATS-Bench extends the benchmark view of NAS by separating two search spaces: topology and size. This is important because many practical architecture improvements come not from new cell graphs, but from depth, width, and channel allocation.

Two Search Spaces

NATS-Bench includes:

Space What varies
topology search space cell connectivity and operations
size search space channel widths and capacity allocation

The figure summarizes many evaluated architectures and their performance patterns. The benchmark is designed to let algorithms be compared without rerunning expensive training.

Why Size Matters

In deployment-oriented model design, channel width is often a first-order variable. A method that only searches cell topology can miss most of the practical design space.

This is why NATS-Bench is useful. It allows researchers to ask whether an optimizer is good at topology search, size search, or both.

Stored Information

The benchmark stores results over multiple datasets and training settings. This allows stable comparisons of query efficiency and cross-dataset behavior.

I would use it to plot best-so-far curves rather than only final accuracy. NAS methods should be judged by how efficiently they use evaluation budget.

Limitations

NATS-Bench still focuses on small image-classification settings. It does not include real hardware latency, LLM serving constraints, or large-scale Transformer training.

Takeaway

NATS-Bench is valuable because it makes size search reproducible. It reminds us that architecture topology is only one part of model design; width and capacity allocation are often just as important.

entry.title: Once-for-All: Train One Network and Specialize it for Efficient Deployment
entry.content:
Cai H, Gan C, Wang T, Zhang Z, Han S. Once-for-All: Train One Network and Specialize it for Efficient Deployment. ICLR 2020.

Paper

Once-for-All (OFA) changes the deployment story of NAS. Instead of searching and training a new model for every device, it trains one elastic supernet. Subnetworks with different depth, width, kernel size, and resolution can then be selected for different latency and memory targets.

Elastic Dimensions

OFA makes the network elastic along several axes:

Dimension Example
depth number of blocks per stage
width channel counts
kernel size 3x3, 5x5, 7x7
resolution input image size

The figure summarizes the central idea: train a once-for-all network, then specialize subnets for different hardware constraints.

Progressive Shrinking

The training process is not a naive “sample random subnetworks forever” recipe. OFA first trains the largest network, then progressively enables smaller kernel sizes, depths, widths, and resolutions.

This order matters. The largest network learns a strong representation first; smaller subnets then inherit and adapt shared weights.

Sandwich Rule And Inplace Distillation

During training, OFA uses:

  • the largest subnet;
  • the smallest subnet;
  • several random subnets.

This is the sandwich rule. The largest subnet can also act as an inplace teacher for smaller subnets, giving soft labels without a separate teacher model.

Specialization

After the supernet is trained, a search procedure selects subnets under device-specific constraints. The expensive part, full model training, is amortized across many deployment targets.

This is the main practical advantage. Real deployment usually involves multiple phones, edge devices, or latency targets, not one fixed constraint.

Limitations

OFA depends on the ranking fidelity of inherited weights. A subnet that looks good inside the supernet should also be good when deployed. That assumption must be validated.

The method is also CNN/mobile-specific. Applying the same idea to Transformers or LLMs is harder because KV cache, tensor parallelism, and decode-time bottlenecks introduce new constraints.

Takeaway

OFA moves NAS from “find one good architecture” to “train a reusable model family.” For deployment, that is often the more valuable problem.

entry.title: PTQ4ViT: Post-Training ViT Quantization
entry.content:
Paper: PTQ4ViT: Post-Training Quantization for Vision Transformers with Twin Uniform Quantization

PTQ4ViT is useful because it does not pretend a ViT is just a CNN with bigger matrices. Attention maps and post-softmax distributions create quantization behavior that CNN PTQ does not handle well.

Motivation

Vision Transformer activations can have sharp and asymmetric distributions. The attention map is especially sensitive because preserving which tokens attend to which other tokens can matter more than minimizing raw element-wise error.

The figure shows distribution behavior that motivates a non-naive quantizer for ViT tensors.

Methodology

The main quantizer is twin uniform quantization. Instead of mapping all values into one uniform interval, the tensor is split into two regions, each with its own uniform grid. This is still hardware-friendlier than arbitrary non-uniform codebooks, but it handles distributions that a single interval fits poorly.

The paper also uses ranking-aware calibration for attention. For attention maps, the relative ordering of important values can be more relevant than the absolute error. This is a transformer-specific PTQ objective.

Results

PTQ4ViT evaluates DeiT/ViT-style models and shows stronger post-training accuracy than naive uniform quantization, especially at lower bit-widths. The results support the paper’s main claim: ViT PTQ needs attention-aware treatment.

Takeaway

PTQ4ViT belongs in the quantization timeline because it marks the shift from CNN assumptions to transformer assumptions. That same shift later becomes more severe in LLMs, where activation outliers and attention/KV behavior dominate deployment choices.

Why Attention Ranking Matters

For attention, the absolute value error is not always the right metric. If quantization changes which tokens receive the largest attention weights, downstream representations can change even when the average error is small.

That is why PTQ4ViT includes ranking-aware thinking. It tries to preserve the ordering structure that attention uses for token mixing.

Connection To LLMs

This is an early signal that transformer PTQ is not solved by CNN recipes. In LLMs, the same mismatch becomes more severe: attention operates over long contexts, activations have persistent outliers, and KV cache grows over time. PTQ4ViT is a smaller-scale example of the architecture-specific quantization problem.

Source-Level Notes

PTQ4ViT focuses on why ViTs are not just CNNs with different layers. Attention maps and post-GELU activations can have distributions that are poorly served by a single uniform quantizer. The paper introduces twin uniform quantization to use two intervals rather than forcing the whole tensor into one uniform grid.

The other important part is ranking loss. For attention, preserving exact activation values is less important than preserving which tokens attend to which other tokens. A reconstruction metric should therefore penalize changes in attention ordering, not only pointwise MSE.

Reading Detail

This is a useful warning for LLM quantization too. If a tensor is used to form probabilities or routing scores, value error and decision error are not the same thing. A small perturbation that changes top attention positions can matter more than a larger perturbation in an insensitive dimension.

PTQ4ViT is also a reminder that PTQ can be architecture-specific. The right calibration objective depends on what the tensor does inside the model.

Experiment Reading

For ViTs, attention visualization is a useful debugging tool. If quantization preserves top-1 image accuracy but attention maps become noisy, the method may be relying on downstream redundancy rather than genuinely preserving the model behavior. PTQ4ViT’s ranking loss is motivated by this concern.

Twin uniform quantization should be checked on the tensors it targets. The right question is: does the tensor distribution actually have two regions that benefit from separate grids? If not, the added complexity may not help.

I read PTQ4ViT as a reminder that calibration loss should match tensor semantics. For an attention matrix, preserving rank/order can be more important than minimizing average scalar error.

Reproduction Checklist

For each ViT block, I would save attention maps from the full precision and quantized models, then compare top-k attended token overlap. This directly tests the ranking-loss motivation. If MSE is low but top-k overlap collapses, the quantizer is preserving values but not decisions.

I would also ablate twin uniform quantization on only post-GELU activations and only attention maps. That identifies which tensor distribution actually needs the twin-grid treatment.

Boundary / Failure Mode

The boundary is that ViT calibration objectives may not transfer directly to language models. Attention maps exist in both, but token semantics, sequence lengths, and causal masking differ. I would reuse the idea of ranking-preserving calibration cautiously: first prove that preserving attention order correlates with downstream quality for the target architecture.

entry.title: PC-DARTS: Partial Channel Connections for Memory-Efficient Architecture Search
PowerInfer: Consumer-GPU LLM Serving
entry.content:
Paper: PowerInfer: Fast Large Language Model Serving with a Consumer-grade GPU

PowerInfer targets a different environment from vLLM or DistServe: local serving with a consumer GPU. The constraint is a hard GPU-memory limit, not cluster-level batching.

Motivation

Many LLM feed-forward neurons are not active for every token. If active neurons are predictable, the runtime can keep frequently used parts on GPU and handle colder parts through CPU-GPU hybrid execution.

The figure shows hot/cold neuron placement and the hybrid execution path.

Methodology

PowerInfer profiles activation sparsity and partitions model components into hot and cold regions. Hot neurons stay on GPU for fast access. Cold neurons can be placed on CPU or handled with offloading, reducing GPU memory pressure.

This is not weight quantization. It is placement and execution based on activation sparsity.

Results

The paper reports faster local inference on consumer GPU setups compared with straightforward offloading baselines. The speedup depends on how stable activation sparsity is and how much CPU-GPU transfer overhead can be avoided.

Takeaway

PowerInfer is a local-inference branch of serving research. Datacenter systems optimize batching, KV cache, and SLOs. Consumer-GPU systems optimize around fitting the model into limited GPU memory. Activation sparsity gives another lever besides quantization and paging.

Hot/Cold Placement

PowerInfer depends on activation sparsity being predictable enough to partition neurons. Hot neurons are worth keeping on GPU because they are used frequently. Cold neurons can be offloaded because they are rarely active.

The idea is similar to cache hierarchy: GPU memory is the fast cache, CPU memory is the larger slow store, and activation prediction decides what belongs where.

Different From Quantization

Quantization reduces the size of every weight. PowerInfer reduces effective GPU demand by exploiting which weights are needed for a token. These can be combined, but they solve different problems.

Limitation

The method is workload- and model-dependent. If activation sparsity is weak or unpredictable, CPU-GPU transfers can erase the benefit. It is most relevant for local inference where the model barely exceeds GPU memory.

Source-Level Notes

PowerInfer targets consumer-grade GPU serving by exploiting activation sparsity. In many Transformer feed-forward layers, only a subset of neurons are strongly activated for a given token. The paper separates neurons into hot and cold groups and places them differently across GPU and CPU memory.

A simplified FFN view is:

If many entries of are near zero or predictable as inactive, the system can avoid treating all neurons equally for placement and computation.

Systems Reading

This is different from quantization. Quantization shrinks every weight. PowerInfer changes where computation and weights live based on activation likelihood. Hot neurons stay on GPU for speed; colder parts can be offloaded or handled with less GPU residency.

The limitation is prediction and workload dependence. If the hot/cold split is wrong for a domain, CPU-GPU transfer or missed GPU locality can erase the benefit. The paper is best read as a local-inference/offloading design rather than a datacenter serving baseline like vLLM.

Experiment Reading

The hot-neuron profile should be measured per model and workload. Activation sparsity is not a universal constant. A chat workload, code workload, and math workload can activate different FFN paths. If the hot set shifts, placement decisions need updating.

The predictor overhead also matters. Predicting active neurons must be cheaper than simply computing them on GPU. Otherwise the hybrid path adds complexity without improving latency.

PowerInfer is most useful when GPU memory is the limiting resource and CPU memory is abundant. In a datacenter GPU server with enough HBM, the CPU-GPU split may be less attractive than straightforward batching, quantization, or tensor parallelism.

Reproduction Checklist

The key profile is neuron activation frequency. I would collect activation statistics over representative prompts, choose hot neurons, then test on a different prompt distribution. If the hot set is stable, placement can be static. If it drifts, the system needs adaptation or loses accuracy/performance.

The CPU-GPU transfer path must also be measured directly. A hybrid system can look good in memory accounting but lose time moving cold activations or weights. The right metric is token latency under a fixed consumer GPU memory budget.

Boundary / Failure Mode

The method also assumes the FFN activation pattern is exploitable at serving time. If batching mixes many unrelated prompts, hot neurons across the batch may cover most of the network and reduce sparsity. A good benchmark should include realistic batch composition, not just single-prompt traces where activation locality is easiest to exploit.

entry.title: Primer: Searching for Efficient Transformers for Language Modeling
QLoRA: 4-bit LLM Fine-Tuning
entry.content:
Paper: QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs

QLoRA is a training paper, not just an inference compression paper. Its contribution is making large-model fine-tuning possible on much smaller hardware by quantizing the frozen base model.

Motivation

LoRA reduces trainable parameters, but the base model still occupies GPU memory. Full fine-tuning also needs gradients and optimizer states. QLoRA keeps the base model in 4-bit memory while training small LoRA adapters.

The figure shows the QLoRA stack: quantized frozen weights, LoRA adapters, double quantization, and paged optimizers.

Methodology

QLoRA has three key pieces.

NF4

NormalFloat4 is a 4-bit data type designed for normally distributed weights. Pretrained weights are often close enough to this assumption that NF4 gives lower error than a uniform 4-bit grid.

Double Quantization

The quantization constants themselves take memory. QLoRA quantizes those constants, reducing metadata overhead.

Paged Optimizers

Fine-tuning can create memory spikes, especially with long sequences. Paged optimizers move optimizer state through unified memory to avoid out-of-memory failures.

The base model is frozen. Gradients pass through the quantized weights into LoRA adapters.

Results

QLoRA demonstrates fine-tuning models up to 65B parameters on much more accessible hardware. The Guanaco models are the headline result, showing strong instruction-following quality from 4-bit base fine-tuning.

Takeaway

QLoRA changed what people could fine-tune. Its quantization format is chosen for frozen-weight training memory, not necessarily for fastest inference kernels. That distinction matters: NF4 is excellent for memory-efficient fine-tuning, while deployment systems may prefer INT4/FP8 formats with specialized kernels.

Memory Accounting

QLoRA is best understood through memory accounting. LoRA reduces trainable parameters, but the frozen base still dominates memory. NF4 reduces the base model memory; double quantization reduces scale metadata; paged optimizers reduce transient optimizer spikes.

A simplified comparison:

Fine-tuning mode Base weights Trainable weights Optimizer state
Full fine-tune FP16/BF16 all weights huge
LoRA FP16/BF16 adapters small
QLoRA 4-bit NF4 adapters small + paged

The third row is why 65B fine-tuning becomes accessible.

Deployment Caveat

A QLoRA-trained adapter can be merged or served with a quantized base, but NF4 is primarily a training-memory format. For production inference, the fastest format may be a different INT4/FP8 layout depending on kernels.

Source-Level Notes

QLoRA is a training paper, not just an inference compression paper. The base model is quantized to 4-bit and frozen; LoRA adapters carry the trainable update:

where is the quantized base weight and is a low-rank trainable adapter. Gradients flow through the quantized base into the adapter, but the base weights are not updated.

The NF4 datatype is designed for normally distributed weights. Instead of uniform bins, its codebook places levels according to normal quantiles. Double quantization then quantizes the quantization constants themselves, reducing metadata overhead.

Memory Accounting

The practical contribution is that fine-tuning memory is dominated by optimizer states and activations, not only model weights. QLoRA combines 4-bit base weights, LoRA, paged optimizers, and careful memory management to fit large-model fine-tuning on smaller GPUs.

At inference time, a merged or adapter-based deployment still has to consider kernel support. QLoRA makes fine-tuning cheap; it does not automatically make the final model faster unless the serving stack uses efficient 4-bit kernels.

Experiment Reading

QLoRA should be evaluated on fine-tuning quality and memory, not only perplexity after quantization. The question is whether gradients through a 4-bit frozen base give LoRA adapters enough signal to match higher-precision fine-tuning.

Paged optimizers matter because activation/optimizer memory spikes can exceed the average footprint. A method that fits most steps but OOMs on long sequences is not practically useful. QLoRA’s memory story includes these spikes, not only NF4.

For deployment, I would decide whether to serve with adapters dynamically or merge them into the base representation. Multi-adapter serving changes memory layout and batching behavior, so QLoRA’s training efficiency does not automatically determine serving efficiency.

Reproduction Checklist

To reproduce QLoRA honestly, memory should be tracked during the whole training step: parameters, gradients, optimizer states, activations, and temporary spikes. Peak memory is the number that decides whether fine-tuning fits on a GPU.

I would also compare NF4 with uniform FP4/int4 under the same LoRA rank. If NF4 helps because pretrained weights are roughly normal, that advantage should appear before changing other training settings.

entry.title: RPTQ: Reorder-Based LLM Quantization
entry.content:
Paper: RPTQ: Reorder-Based Post-Training Quantization for Large Language Models

RPTQ is another activation-outlier paper, but it uses a different lever from SmoothQuant. Instead of scaling channels, it reorders them so quantization groups are easier to represent.

Motivation

Group-wise quantization is a compromise: it avoids one scale for the whole tensor but does not require one scale per element. The problem is that if outlier channels are spread across many groups, each group has a large range and poor resolution.

The figure shows how channel reordering changes the grouping structure seen by the quantizer.

Methodology

RPTQ constructs channel permutations that place similar activation channels together. If a permutation can be folded into adjacent linear layers, the model function remains equivalent while the quantizer sees better grouped distributions.

The method is particularly relevant for activations after LayerNorm and other locations where persistent outlier channels appear.

Results

RPTQ reports LLM PTQ results showing better activation quantization than naive grouping. It is not as widely adopted as SmoothQuant or GPTQ, but it is a useful design point: data layout itself can be a quantization parameter.

Takeaway

The main lesson is that group boundaries matter. Once the runtime quantizes by group, channel order affects accuracy even if the mathematical model is unchanged. QuaRot later generalizes this idea: instead of only reordering coordinates, rotate the basis to spread outliers more evenly.

Reordering Is A Layout Transformation

RPTQ is easy to underestimate because channel reordering sounds trivial. But if quantization is group-wise, the grouping layout changes the scale statistics. Moving outlier channels together can prevent them from polluting every group.

The transformation is useful only if it can be folded into adjacent layers or supported cheaply by the runtime. Otherwise the model may save quantization error but pay layout-conversion overhead.

Relation To QuaRot

RPTQ permutes coordinates. QuaRot applies an orthogonal rotation. Both are equivalent transformations before quantization, but rotation has more freedom to spread outlier energy. RPTQ is cheaper; QuaRot is stronger.

Source-Level Notes

RPTQ attacks activation outliers through channel reordering. If outlier channels are scattered, a group-wise quantizer has to use a large scale for many ordinary channels. If channels are reordered so similar ranges fall into the same group, group quantization wastes less resolution.

A permutation can preserve the network function when it is propagated consistently:

The challenge is not the algebra; it is carrying compatible permutations through Transformer blocks without breaking residual paths and normalization assumptions.

Reading Detail

RPTQ is useful because it treats layout as part of quantization. Quantization quality is not only about choosing bit width and scale. It can also depend on which channels share a scale group.

QuaRot later takes a more continuous version of this idea: instead of permuting channels, rotate them with an orthogonal transform to spread outliers. RPTQ is therefore a good bridge between SmoothQuant-style scaling and QuaRot-style rotations.

Experiment Reading

The key experiment is whether reordering improves group quantization at the same group size. If group size is one, reordering is irrelevant. If group size is large, reordering can decide whether ordinary channels share a scale with outliers.

I would also check the cost of carrying permutations through the model. A permutation that introduces runtime shuffles can erase benefits. The strongest form is one where permutations are fused into adjacent weights or handled as a static layout transform.

RPTQ is therefore a layout-aware quantization method. It does not invent a new numeric type; it makes an existing group quantizer see friendlier groups.

Reproduction Checklist

For a small reproduction I would start with one Transformer block and record activation ranges before and after reordering. The expected result is that channels inside each quantization group have more similar magnitudes after permutation. Then I would fold the permutation into adjacent linear weights and verify that the floating-point output is unchanged before quantization. That check separates algebraic correctness from quantization benefit.

The final benchmark should report whether any runtime transpose or gather remains. RPTQ is attractive only if reordering becomes a static layout choice. If every token pays a dynamic shuffle cost, the method can lose the simplicity that made it appealing.

Boundary / Failure Mode

The limitation is that permutations are discrete and preserve only reordered axes. If outliers are not just misplaced but genuinely concentrated in a few semantic dimensions, reordering can only group them; it cannot reduce their magnitude. That is where SmoothQuant-style scaling or QuaRot-style rotation becomes stronger. RPTQ is best when group-wise quantization is already required and layout can be changed almost for free.

entry.title: RoBERTa: A Robustly Optimized BERT Pretraining Approach
entry.content:
Paper

RoBERTa 是一篇很适合校准判断的论文。它没有提出复杂新结构，而是系统复现并强化 BERT 训练 recipe：更多数据、更大 batch、更长训练、动态 masking、去掉 NSP。结论是很多 post-BERT 方法的收益可能混入了训练不足和数据规模差异。

Dynamic Masking

BERT 原始实现会在数据预处理阶段生成固定 mask。RoBERTa 改成动态 masking，每次喂入序列时重新采样 mask。表 1 里动态 mask 和静态 mask 差距不巨大，但在更长训练和更多 epoch 下更合理，因为模型不会反复看到完全相同的 corruption pattern。

Recipe

RoBERTa 的主要改动：

  • 训练更久，batch 更大；
  • 使用更多文本数据，不只 BookCorpus + Wikipedia；
  • 去掉 Next Sentence Prediction；
  • 用更长序列训练；
  • byte-level BPE 词表。

去掉 NSP 是最被记住的一点，但我觉得更重要的是论文的方法论：比较预训练方法时必须控制 compute、data、batch、steps，否则“新目标函数”的收益很可能只是训练更充分。

Takeaway

RoBERTa 把 BERT 从一个模型名字变成了一个强训练基线。它提醒后续论文：如果只是换了 objective 或小结构，但没有和强 recipe 下的 BERT/RoBERTa 比，结论很容易被高估。

entry.title: S3: ViT Search Space Search
entry.content:
Chen M, Peng H, Fu J, Ling H. Searching the Search Space of Vision Transformer.

Paper

S3-ViT asks a higher-level question: before searching for an architecture, how good is the search space? Many NAS methods assume a fixed search space, but a poor space can make even a strong optimizer look bad.

Problem Formulation

The method evaluates and improves ViT search spaces. A good search space should contain strong architectures, but it should also be searchable. If only a tiny number of candidates are good, random or cheap search will struggle.

The figure shows the pipeline: decompose the search space, evaluate each dimension, and evolve the search space itself.

E-T Error

The paper uses an error metric that considers both top quality and search difficulty. The point is to avoid spaces that contain one excellent architecture but are otherwise full of poor candidates.

This is a useful distinction:

Space property Why it matters
top architecture quality determines the best possible result
average candidate quality affects random and cheap search
dimension usefulness avoids wasting search budget
scalability matters for larger ViT variants

ViT-Specific Dimensions

ViT design dimensions include stage depth, embedding width, attention heads, MLP ratio, and token resolution. These dimensions interact. A search space that treats them independently may include many invalid or weak configurations.

Takeaway

S3 is a meta-NAS paper. It argues that search-space engineering is not a preliminary detail; it is part of the NAS problem. For ViTs, this matters because the design dimensions are strongly coupled.

entry.title: SARATHI: Chunked Prefill Scheduling
entry.content:
Paper: SARATHI: Efficient LLM Inference by Piggybacking Decodes with Chunked Prefills

SARATHI focuses on a scheduling problem: prefill and decode have very different shapes. A long prefill is compute-heavy and parallel. Decode is iterative, one token per sequence, and latency-sensitive.

Motivation

Serving metrics are usually split into:

  • TTFT: time to first token, dominated by prefill;
  • TPOT: time per output token, dominated by decode;
  • throughput: completed tokens or requests per second.

If a scheduler runs a long prefill as one monolithic batch, decode requests can wait too long. If it prioritizes decode too aggressively, GPU utilization can fall.

The figure shows SARATHI’s basic idea: split long prefills into chunks and mix them with decode work.

Methodology

SARATHI uses chunked prefill. Instead of processing an entire prompt in one step, it divides the prompt into smaller chunks. Decode tokens from active requests can piggyback with these chunks.

The scheduler tries to create decode-maximal batches:

  1. include decode work to protect TPOT;
  2. fill remaining compute capacity with prefill chunks;
  3. avoid letting one long prompt monopolize the GPU.

This differs from PagedAttention. vLLM solves KV memory allocation; SARATHI solves the phase-mixing problem between prefill and decode.

Results

The paper reports better latency-throughput behavior on workloads with long or variable prompts. Chunking reduces stalls caused by monolithic prefills and improves GPU utilization compared with naive phase scheduling.

Takeaway

SARATHI is a scheduler paper about the shape mismatch in LLM inference. It is useful to read before DistServe: SARATHI mixes prefill and decode more carefully on the same workers, while DistServe separates the phases onto different workers.

Prefill/Decode Interference

A useful mental model is that prefill wants large matrix-multiply batches, while decode wants predictable per-token service. If decode waits behind long prefill, TPOT becomes bad. If prefill is always interrupted, TTFT and throughput become bad.

Chunked prefill creates smaller scheduling units. This lets the scheduler interleave work without throwing away GPU utilization.

What The Scheduler Is Really Optimizing

The scheduler is not simply maximizing tokens/s. It is balancing two latency distributions. A system can have high aggregate throughput and still be unusable if decode tokens arrive with high jitter. SARATHI’s decode-maximal batching protects active conversations while still admitting prefill work.

Boundary With DistServe

SARATHI keeps phases on the same hardware and changes scheduling. DistServe changes the architecture by separating phase resources. SARATHI has less KV transfer overhead; DistServe has more independent scaling.

Source-Level Notes

SARATHI studies the interference between prefill and decode. Prefill processes many prompt tokens in parallel and is compute-heavy. Decode processes one new token per sequence and is often memory/KV-cache bound. Naively mixing them can hurt both TTFT and TPOT.

The paper’s main idea is chunked prefill: split a long prompt into chunks and piggyback those chunks with decode batches. The scheduler tries to remain decode-maximal, meaning decode tokens keep making progress while prefill work fills otherwise underused compute.

Scheduler Reading

The method is not only batching. It changes the unit of scheduling from whole prompts to prompt chunks. That lets a long prompt stop monopolizing the GPU before existing decode requests get their next token.

The relationship with DistServe is useful. SARATHI keeps prefill and decode on the same serving workers but schedules them more carefully. DistServe later argues that the two phases are different enough to place on separate resources. Both papers start from the same observation: prefill and decode stress hardware differently.

Experiment Reading

The result curves should be read across request length distributions. Chunked prefill matters most when prompts are long enough to block decode progress. If prompts are uniformly short, the scheduler has less room to improve over ordinary batching.

TTFT and TPOT can move in opposite directions. A scheduler that prioritizes prefill may improve TTFT but hurt ongoing decode latency. SARATHI’s decode-maximal framing is useful because it treats decode progress as the steady-state heartbeat of the system.

A reproduction should log GPU utilization by phase. The goal is not just larger batches; it is filling compute slack from decode with prefill chunks without making decode wait too long.

Reproduction Checklist

The scheduler should log how many prefill chunks and decode tokens are placed in each iteration. If decode batches are often delayed by large prefill chunks, the implementation is not decode-maximal. If prefill chunks are too small, overhead can dominate.

I would sweep chunk size. The best value depends on prompt length distribution and GPU. This is a scheduling parameter, not a universal constant from the paper.

entry.title: SGLang: Structured LLM Runtime
entry.content:
Paper: SGLang: Efficient Execution of Structured Language Model Programs

SGLang targets LLM applications that are programs, not isolated completions. A workflow may branch, call tools, enforce schemas, or evaluate multiple candidates with shared prefixes. A normal API recomputes too much.

Motivation

Many prompts share prefixes:

  • few-shot examples reused across calls;
  • retrieved context reused across subquestions;
  • tree search or agent branches sharing history;
  • constrained decoding with structured output.

If the runtime throws away prefix KV cache, it wastes prefill work.

The figure shows the runtime/programming model and how structured generation exposes reuse opportunities.

Methodology

The core system idea is RadixAttention. KV cache is stored in a radix tree keyed by token prefix. If a new request shares a prefix with an existing cache path, the runtime reuses those KV blocks.

SGLang also provides a frontend language for expressing multi-call generation programs. This matters because the runtime needs to see the program structure to batch and reuse effectively.

Results

The paper reports significant speedups on structured generation workloads compared with ordinary serving. The gain comes from avoiding repeated prefill and improving batching across program fragments.

Takeaway

vLLM optimizes memory management for independent dynamic requests. SGLang adds a program-level cache reuse layer. For RAG, agents, and structured decoding, the runtime should know that repeated prefixes are not accidental; they are part of the program.

RadixAttention As Prefix Cache

A radix tree is a natural structure for shared prefixes. If prompts share the token sequence , the KV cache for that prefix can be stored once. Branches only need to compute after the divergence point.

This is especially useful for:

  • best-of-N sampling from the same prompt;
  • tree search in reasoning systems;
  • tool-call branches sharing conversation history;
  • RAG workflows reusing the same retrieved context.

Programming Model Matters

The runtime can only exploit structure it can see. If an application issues independent HTTP calls with duplicated prompts, the server may not know they are related. SGLang’s frontend exposes program structure so the runtime can schedule and reuse KV cache.

Limitation

Cache reuse helps when prefixes repeat. For unrelated single-turn prompts, SGLang’s program-level advantage is smaller, and ordinary vLLM-style batching may be enough.

Source-Level Notes

SGLang is built around structured language model programs. Real LLM applications often branch, call tools, reuse prefixes, enforce formats, or sample multiple continuations. A runtime that only sees independent strings misses reuse opportunities.

RadixAttention stores KV cache in a radix tree keyed by token prefixes. If two requests share a prefix, the runtime can reuse the corresponding KV cache rather than recomputing it.

Runtime Reading

The key insight is that prefix reuse should be visible to the scheduler. In a normal batch API, two prompts with a shared prefix may arrive as unrelated requests. In SGLang, the program structure exposes forks and joins, so the runtime can plan reuse.

This complements vLLM rather than replacing it. PagedAttention solves block allocation and continuous batching. SGLang adds a program/runtime layer that makes structured generation and cache reuse explicit.

Experiment Reading

SGLang’s gains depend on structured workloads. If requests are independent one-shot prompts, RadixAttention has fewer prefixes to reuse. If applications branch, sample, verify, call tools, or share long system prompts, the radix tree can save substantial prefill work.

The programming model matters because it exposes structure before execution. A normal API receives strings; SGLang receives a program with control flow. That gives the runtime more information for cache reuse and scheduling.

A reproduction should include workloads with shared prefixes and branching. Otherwise the evaluation only tests the backend as another batch server and misses the main point of the paper.

Reproduction Checklist

The minimal test case should include shared prefixes and branching. For example, run several prompts with the same system prefix, then fork multiple continuations from an intermediate state. A plain batching benchmark will not show RadixAttention’s main value.

I would log prefix-cache hit rate, saved prefill tokens, and memory occupied by cached KV nodes. Cache reuse is not free; old prefixes compete with new requests for memory. A good runtime needs both reuse and eviction behavior to be visible in metrics.

Boundary / Failure Mode

The failure case is low reuse. If prompts do not share prefixes and programs do not branch, RadixAttention mainly adds cache-management complexity. The runtime needs to detect when reuse is worth storing and when cached prefixes should be evicted. This is why SGLang is best understood as an application-runtime paper: the more structure the application exposes, the more the backend can exploit.

entry.title: Single-Path NAS: Designing Hardware-Efficient ConvNets in Less Than 4 Hours
SpQR: Sparse-Quantized LLM Weights
entry.content:
Paper: SpQR: A Sparse-Quantized Representation for Near-Lossless LLM Weight Compression

SpQR is an outlier-aware weight compression method. Instead of forcing every weight into one dense low-bit representation, it separates the hard weights into a sparse component.

Motivation

A small number of weights can dominate quantization error. If the dense quantizer expands its range to include them, it wastes precision for normal weights. If it ignores them, perplexity degrades. SpQR uses a sparse-plus-dense representation.

The figure visualizes sensitivity and outlier handling. The core idea is to let the dense quantizer do the common case and store exceptional weights separately.

Methodology

The representation is:

  • dense low-bit quantized weights for the majority of entries;
  • sparse higher-precision values for outlier/sensitive entries;
  • metadata that identifies where sparse corrections apply.

This is related to LLM.int8() conceptually, but the object is different. LLM.int8() isolates activation outlier dimensions at runtime. SpQR isolates weight outliers in the stored model.

Results

SpQR reports near-lossless compression for LLaMA and Falcon-style models at low average bit-widths. The method can achieve strong perplexity because the sparse component catches the weights that a dense codebook handles badly.

Takeaway

SpQR is a quality-oriented compression format. The tradeoff is runtime complexity: sparse corrections must be handled efficiently. If the serving stack cannot exploit the representation, a simpler W4 format may be faster despite slightly worse compression quality.

Sparse Corrections Are A Format Choice

SpQR is not just “quantize with outlier handling”. It defines a representation with a dense quantized matrix plus sparse correction values. That means quality and runtime are coupled to sparse metadata handling.

If the sparse component is too large, metadata and irregular access hurt. If it is too small, important outliers remain in the dense quantizer and perplexity worsens.

When I Would Use This Idea

I would consider SpQR-style formats when near-lossless compression matters more than having the simplest possible kernel path. For maximum throughput on commodity kernels, regular W4 group-wise formats are often easier.

Source-Level Notes

SpQR argues that a tiny set of weights can cause disproportionate quantization error. It defines sensitivity using the best possible compensation by other weights. In the paper’s notation, a weight sensitivity can be written as:

$$
s_{ij} = \min_{W’} |WX - W’X|2^2 \quad \text{s.t.} \quad w’{ij}=\operatorname{quant}(w_{ij})
$$

Using the Hessian view, this becomes tied to the squared rounding error divided by an inverse-Hessian term. High-sensitivity weights are extracted as sparse outliers and stored with higher precision; the rest are quantized to 3-4 bits.

Format Reading

The method is a representation as much as an algorithm. Dense low-bit weights provide compression and throughput. Sparse high-precision outliers preserve accuracy. Quantization metadata such as scales is also compressed to keep the effective bits per parameter low.

The deployment tradeoff is kernel complexity. SpQR can be near-lossless, but the runtime must combine dense low-bit matmul with sparse correction efficiently. If the sparse path is poorly implemented, the accuracy win may not translate into serving speed.

Experiment Reading

The near-lossless claim should be read together with effective bits per parameter. Storing outliers in higher precision and storing metadata both cost bits. A fair comparison asks how much memory is used after all sparse indices, scales, and codebooks are counted.

The paper’s sensitivity definition is useful because it avoids a naive view of outliers. A large absolute weight is not automatically important; a weight is important if quantizing it causes output error that cannot be compensated by other weights.

For runtime, I would profile dense and sparse parts separately. The sparse correction path may be small in FLOPs but expensive in irregular memory access. Good SpQR performance depends on making that correction path GPU-friendly.

Reproduction Checklist

The outlier detector should be evaluated by removing the sparse path after encoding. If perplexity jumps sharply, the extracted weights are truly important. If it barely changes, the sparse path may be wasting metadata.

I would also calculate effective bits per parameter explicitly: dense low-bit weights, scales, zero-points or codebooks, sparse indices, and sparse values. SpQR’s near-lossless claim is meaningful only when this accounting is included.

Boundary / Failure Mode

The failure mode is sparse-path dominance. If a model or bit width requires too many outliers, the sparse correction no longer looks like a small exception path. It becomes a second representation that competes with the dense one. I would set an explicit outlier budget and plot perplexity versus sparse density to see where the method stops being efficient.

entry.title: SqueezeLLM: Dense-and-Sparse Quantization
entry.content:
Paper: SqueezeLLM: Dense-and-Sparse Quantization

SqueezeLLM is another dense-plus-sparse LLM compression method, with more emphasis on non-uniform quantization and serving bandwidth.

Motivation

Weight-only LLM inference is often limited by reading weights from memory. Low-bit weights help, but uniform 3-bit quantization can hurt perplexity. SqueezeLLM improves the low-bit representation by combining a better dense codebook with sparse handling for exceptional values.

The first figure shows the quality improvement from sensitivity-based non-uniform quantization and dense-and-sparse decomposition.

Methodology

The method has two components:

  1. Sensitivity-based non-uniform quantization. Quantization bins are placed closer to sensitive values instead of uniformly across the range.
  2. Dense-and-sparse decomposition. Outlier and sensitive values that are poorly represented by the dense codebook are stored in a sparse full-precision component.

This is similar in spirit to SpQR, but the paper emphasizes the combination of non-uniform dense quantization and sparse corrections.

Results

SqueezeLLM reports improved perplexity at 3-bit and 4-bit settings for LLaMA-style models. The figure highlights that a 3-bit SqueezeLLM model can approach the quality of larger baselines at much lower memory.

Takeaway

SqueezeLLM is useful when the quality target is near-lossless compression at very low average bit-width. The engineering question remains the same as SpQR: can the runtime decode non-uniform dense weights and sparse corrections fast enough to beat simpler quantization formats?

Dense-And-Sparse Compared With SpQR

Both SqueezeLLM and SpQR separate difficult weights from ordinary weights. SqueezeLLM emphasizes sensitivity-aware non-uniform dense quantization, while SpQR emphasizes near-lossless sparse-quantized representation.

The shared bet is that the outlier set is small. If many weights require sparse correction, the method stops being efficient.

Result Interpretation

The headline improvement in perplexity is most meaningful at 3-bit. At 4-bit, several methods are already strong. At 3-bit, non-uniform bins and sparse corrections become more valuable because the dense codebook has very little capacity.

Source-Level Notes

SqueezeLLM also uses a dense-and-sparse view, but emphasizes sensitivity-weighted non-uniform quantization. Instead of assigning uniform bins, the quantizer can minimize a weighted error:

where measures sensitivity, often derived from calibration statistics or Hessian-like information. Large-error or high-sensitivity weights can be separated into a sparse component, leaving the dense component easier to quantize.

Reading Detail

This paper is useful in the GPTQ/AWQ/SpQR neighborhood because it shows another axis: the quantization grid itself can be non-uniform. Uniform 4-bit is simple for kernels, but non-uniform codebooks can better match weight distributions.

The cost is decode complexity. A non-uniform format needs lookup or specialized kernels. Therefore the paper should be judged on both perplexity and implemented inference speed, not only compression ratio.

Experiment Reading

SqueezeLLM’s dense-and-sparse split should be compared with SpQR under the same memory budget. Both protect difficult weights, but the dense representation and sparse correction details differ. The right metric is not only perplexity, but perplexity at a target effective bit rate and measured generation speed.

Non-uniform quantization is attractive when weights are not well matched by uniform bins. The downside is that each code may need decoding through a codebook. If the codebook lookup is not fused efficiently, the memory savings can be offset by extra instructions.

I read this paper as a reminder that 4-bit is not one format. Uniform int4, NF4, non-uniform codebooks, GPTQ-packed weights, AWQ-scaled weights, and sparse-quantized formats all have different kernel consequences.

Reproduction Checklist

I would reproduce the method in three stages. First run uniform group quantization to establish the baseline. Second replace uniform bins with the sensitivity-aware non-uniform codebook and measure perplexity at the same effective bit rate. Third add the sparse correction path and count the real memory overhead from indices and outlier values.

This ordering matters because it tells whether the gain comes from the dense codebook or from sparse outlier storage. It also prevents a misleading comparison where the sparse method silently uses more bits per parameter than the baseline.

Boundary / Failure Mode

The risk is format fragmentation. If every compression method needs its own packing, codebook lookup, sparse correction, and kernel path, deployment becomes hard to maintain. SqueezeLLM is compelling when the accuracy target really requires non-uniform dense quantization plus sparse values. If uniform AWQ or GPTQ already meets the target, the simpler kernel format may be the better engineering choice.
