Paper

T5 不只是一个模型名，它更像一份大型 transfer learning 实验报告。论文把所有任务都写成 text-to-text：输入是带任务前缀的文本，输出也是文本。这样分类、翻译、摘要、问答都用同一个 encoder-decoder Transformer 和同一个 maximum likelihood 目标。

Text-to-Text Interface

这个接口的好处是工程上极其统一。比如 translate English to German: ... 输出德语句子，cola sentence: ... 输出 acceptable 或 not acceptable。模型不需要任务专属 head，任务信息通过自然语言前缀进入输入。

Objective Survey

T5 系统比较了 language modeling、masked language modeling、prefix LM、span corruption 等目标。最终常用的是 span corruption：随机选若干连续 span，用 sentinel token 替换，decoder 生成被替换的 spans。

span corruption 相比逐 token MLM 更适合 seq2seq，因为 decoder 需要生成一串被遮盖文本，而不是独立分类每个 token。它也比普通 LM 更适合 encoder-decoder：encoder 看到 corrupted input，decoder 学重建 missing spans。

Data and Scale

T5 引入 C4 数据集，对 Common Crawl 做清洗过滤。论文的实验范围很大：模型规模、训练步数、数据集大小、multi-task mixing、fine-tuning 策略都被系统比较。这里最值得学的是实验组织方式，而不只是最终分数。

Takeaway

T5 的贡献有三层：

  1. 统一任务接口：所有 NLP 任务都变成 text-to-text。
  2. 统一模型结构：encoder-decoder Transformer 处理输入和输出。
  3. 统一实验框架：在同一设置下比较目标、数据和规模。

后来的 instruction tuning 和 prompt 模板都继承了这个思路：不要为每个任务重写网络，把任务描述变成模型输入的一部分。

entry.title: Neural Architecture Search on ImageNet in Four GPU Hours: A Theoretically Inspired Perspective
TernaryBERT: Distilled Ternary BERT
entry.content:
Paper: TernaryBERT: Distillation-aware Ultra-low Bit BERT

TernaryBERT pushes BERT into a very low-bit regime. At ternary precision, ordinary fine-tuning is usually not enough. The model needs a teacher.

Motivation

BERT is expensive for edge NLP or high-throughput inference. INT8 compression helps, but ternary weights and activations promise much larger memory reduction. The cost is representational capacity: a ternary student is too constrained to learn only from task labels.

The schematic above is a local redraw of the method path: a full-precision teacher supervises a ternary student through several losses. Distillation is not an optional improvement; it is part of making the quantized model trainable.

Methodology

The student uses ternary quantization, typically values like for weights or activations:

Here is the threshold that decides whether a value is suppressed to zero, and is the retained ternary scale. The exact threshold/scale policy can vary by tensor, but the important point is that most magnitude information is removed.

The training objective combines several forms of distillation:

  • prediction-layer distillation from teacher logits;
  • hidden-state distillation to preserve intermediate representations;
  • attention or transformer-layer distillation so the internal computation does not drift too far.

This makes TernaryBERT different from PTQ. It is a quantized student training method.

Results

The paper evaluates on GLUE-style tasks and shows that ternary BERT can keep much more accuracy with distillation than naive ternary baselines. The model is still not exactly full precision, but the compression ratio is large and the degradation is controlled.

Takeaway

TernaryBERT is useful for understanding the boundary between quantization and model compression. At 8-bit, QAT may be enough. At ternary or binary precision, the student often needs teacher supervision because the function class has changed too much.

For current LLM deployment, 4-bit weight-only PTQ is usually more practical than ternary full-model quantization. Still, TernaryBERT explains why distillation keeps showing up in aggressive compression papers.

Distillation Granularity

The paper does not rely only on final logits. For a transformer student, matching intermediate hidden states and attention behavior is important because errors can compound across layers. This is especially true at ternary precision, where the student has much less capacity.

A useful way to read the loss is:

$$
\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{task} + \lambda_1\mathcal{L}{logit} + \lambda_2\mathcal{L}{hidden} + \lambda_3\mathcal{L}{attention}
$$

The exact weights are implementation details, but the decomposition shows why the method works: the teacher constrains the student at multiple depths.

Where It Fits

TernaryBERT sits between Q8BERT and BinaryBERT. It is more aggressive than 8-bit QAT, but less extreme than binary compression. It shows that as bit-width decreases, quantization becomes increasingly entangled with knowledge distillation.

Source-Level Notes

TernaryBERT pushes BERT weights and activations toward three-level representations, usually of the form:

At this precision, direct fine-tuning is not enough. The paper relies on knowledge distillation so the ternary student learns from a full-precision teacher. The distillation signal is applied beyond final logits; intermediate Transformer representations are also important because quantization noise accumulates through attention and feed-forward blocks.

This is the part I would not simplify away. A ternary BERT is not just a full-precision BERT with smaller storage. Its representational surface is different. Distillation gives the low-capacity student many local targets inside the Transformer, so it does not have to discover the teacher’s behavior only from task labels.

Reading Detail

The paper is best read as a compression recipe, not only a quantizer. Ternary quantization supplies the compact representation, while distillation supplies the optimization signal that keeps the student close to BERT behavior.

The limitation is that ternary arithmetic only helps if the deployment stack can exploit it. Otherwise the method can reduce model storage but fail to deliver proportional latency improvements. This is a recurring theme in ultra-low-bit NLP quantization: accuracy papers and kernel/runtime papers have to meet.

Experiment Reading

At ternary precision, the student has very little capacity to exactly match the teacher. The important question is which distillation losses are used. Logit-only distillation may preserve final predictions but allow hidden states to drift. Intermediate-layer distillation constrains attention and feed-forward representations, which is usually necessary for stable BERT compression.

I would also inspect whether weights and activations are both ternary. Weight-only ternarization mainly reduces model storage. Activation ternarization changes the compute path and usually creates a larger accuracy challenge.

The paper is a good reminder that low-bit NLP compression is often a package: quantization format, initialization, distillation, and fine-tuning schedule all matter. Removing one piece can make the bit-width headline misleading.

Reproduction Checklist

A useful ablation separates quantization and distillation. Train a ternary model with labels only, then add logit distillation, then add intermediate representation distillation. The gap shows how much of the result comes from teacher supervision rather than the ternary format alone.

I would also record activation quantization error across layers. If one or two layers dominate the error, mixed precision or keeping specific operators higher precision may be a better deployment compromise than uniformly ternarizing everything.

entry.title: TransNAS-Bench-101: Improving Transferability and Generalizability of Cross-Task NAS
entry.content:
Duan Y, Chen X, Xu H, et al. TransNAS-Bench-101: Improving Transferability and Generalizability of Cross-Task NAS.

Paper

TransNAS-Bench-101 moves NAS benchmarking beyond single-task image classification. It evaluates architectures across multiple vision tasks, making it possible to ask whether architecture knowledge transfers.

This is an important shift. A cell that works well for classification may not be best for segmentation, depth prediction, or surface normal estimation.

Search Spaces

The benchmark includes both micro-level cell choices and macro-level skeleton choices.

The figure shows the cell-level and macro-level search spaces, as well as the task-specific decoders. The benchmark explicitly includes the interaction between architecture and task.

Why Cross-Task Matters

Real vision backbones are often reused across tasks. A model may need to support classification, detection, segmentation, and dense prediction. If a NAS method only works on one classification dataset, it may not discover generally useful architectures.

Transfer Questions

The benchmark lets us ask:

  • Does ranking correlate across tasks?
  • Does a cell found on one task transfer to another?
  • Are macro skeleton choices more important than micro cells?
  • Do some architectures specialize strongly by task?

These questions are more realistic than only optimizing CIFAR classification error.

Limitations

The benchmark is still controlled and limited compared with large-scale real training. It should be used for diagnosis, not as a final replacement for task-specific evaluation.

Takeaway

TransNAS-Bench-101 is valuable because it reframes NAS as architecture-task interaction. General NAS claims should be tested on cross-task benchmarks, not only on small classification cell spaces.

An Image is Worth 16x16 Words: Transformers for Image Recognition at Scale
ViTAS: Vision Transformer Architecture Search
entry.content:
Su X, You S, Xie J, et al. Vision Transformer Architecture Search. ECCV 2022.

Paper

ViTAS studies NAS for Vision Transformers. Transformer NAS is not just CNN NAS with different blocks. Width, heads, MLP ratio, token resolution, and stage design interact differently, and one-shot weight sharing can become fragile.

Why Transformer NAS Is Different

In CNN NAS, channel sharing and operation choices are already difficult. In ViT supernets, channel fairness becomes even more important because attention and MLP projections depend strongly on embedding dimensions.

The figure compares ordinary channel sharing and cyclic channel sharing. Cyclic sharing tries to ensure that different channels receive more balanced training.

Cyclic Weight Sharing

If smaller subnets always use the first channels, those channels are trained more often than later channels. This creates unfair inherited weights and unreliable subnet ranking.

Cyclic sharing rotates channel usage so that different subnets train different channel slices. The goal is to reduce ranking bias inside the supernet.

Search Dimensions

ViTAS searches dimensions such as:

  • embedding/channel width;
  • attention heads;
  • MLP ratio;
  • depth;
  • stage structure.

These dimensions are coupled. For example, changing embedding dimension affects head dimension and MLP cost.

Results And Interpretation

The paper reports strong results on ImageNet and downstream vision tasks. The more reusable lesson is that Transformer supernet training must control channel sampling bias. Otherwise the search algorithm may simply select architectures that received better shared weights.

Takeaway

ViTAS is important because it treats supernet fairness as a core problem. For Transformer NAS, reliable ranking is at least as important as the size of the search space.

entry.title: XLNet: Generalized Autoregressive Pretraining for Language Understanding
entry.content:
Paper

XLNet 是 BERT 之后一个很有代表性的目标函数改造。它的批评点是：BERT 的 MLM 会引入 [MASK] 预训练/微调不一致，并且被 mask 的 token 之间条件独立。XLNet 想保留 autoregressive likelihood 的严谨性，同时通过排列分解顺序让每个位置看到双向上下文。

Permutation LM

XLNet 最大化所有 factorization order 的期望：

$$
\max_\theta \mathbb{E}{z\sim \mathcal{Z}T}\left[\sum{t=1}^{T}\log p_\theta(x{z_t}\mid x_{z_{<t}})\right]
$$

这里 是位置排列。注意输入序列本身不打乱，只是 attention mask 按排列顺序决定哪些 token 可见。因此某个 token 在某些排列中可以看到左侧和右侧上下文。

Two-stream Attention

naive permutation LM 有一个问题：预测位置 时，query 不能看到自己的内容 ，但 hidden state 又需要知道当前位置。XLNet 用两条 stream 解决：content stream 编码内容，query stream 编码“要预测的位置”但不泄漏该位置内容。

XLNet 还直接引入 Transformer-XL 的 segment recurrence 和 relative position，因此长上下文能力比普通 BERT-style encoder 更强。

Reading Notes

XLNet 的优点是目标函数更接近真正 likelihood，避免 [MASK]。缺点是实现和训练更复杂，两条 stream 加排列 mask 的工程成本高。后来的 RoBERTa 说明 BERT 如果用更多数据、更大 batch、更长训练，也能非常强。因此 XLNet 更像是“目标函数探索”的重要分支，而不是最终替代 BERT 的路线。

Takeaway

XLNet 值得记住三点：

  • 用 permutation order 获得双向上下文，而不是 corruption；
  • two-stream attention 防止 target token 内容泄漏；
  • 与 Transformer-XL 结合，说明位置编码和 recurrence 可以服务于预训练目标。

它对理解 BERT/GPT 目标函数差异很有帮助：不是所有双向上下文都必须通过 MLM 得到，也不是所有 autoregressive 都只能左到右。

entry.title: Zen-NAS: A Zero-Shot NAS for High-Performance Deep Image Recognition
entry.content:
Lin M, Wang P, Sun Z, et al. Zen-NAS: A Zero-Shot NAS for High-Performance Deep Image Recognition. ICCV 2021.

Paper

Zen-NAS is a zero-shot NAS method for CNN image recognition. It scores architectures using an initialization-time expressivity measure, avoiding candidate training during search.

The paper is interesting because it pushes the idea of training-free architecture search further than ordinary cheap proxies.

Zen-Score Intuition

The central idea is to measure how sensitively a randomly initialized network responds to input perturbations. If a network produces rich and distinguishable activations at initialization, it may have stronger representational capacity after training.

The figure shows the accuracy-latency comparison of ZenNets against other CNN families. The method aims to find strong Pareto points with very low search cost.

Search Setup

Zen-NAS searches in a constrained CNN space. This constraint is important. The zero-shot score is meaningful only when the search space is regular enough that the proxy’s assumptions hold.

The method is less obviously applicable to arbitrary DAGs, dense skip structures, or Transformer blocks.

BatchNorm And Scale

Initialization-time scores can be distorted by normalization and scale. Zen-NAS pays attention to how the network is evaluated at initialization. Without consistent handling, proxy scores may reflect numerical artifacts rather than architecture quality.

Results

The paper reports strong ImageNet accuracy-latency Pareto results with low search cost. The most important claim is not just speed, but that a carefully designed zero-shot score can guide search in a well-structured CNN space.

Limitations

Zen-Score is not a universal theory of generalization. It is a practical proxy under a strong search-space prior. If the space is irregular, the score may be unreliable.

Takeaway

Zen-NAS shows that training-free search can work when the architecture space is designed around the assumptions of the proxy. The search space and the score have to be read together.

entry.title: Zero-Cost Proxies for Lightweight NAS
entry.content:
Abdelfattah M S, Mehrotra A, Dudziak L, Lane N D. Zero-Cost Proxies for Lightweight NAS.

Paper

Zero-cost NAS asks whether an architecture can be scored without training. Instead of training each candidate, it computes cheap signals at initialization, often using gradients, saliency, or Jacobian statistics.

The goal is not to perfectly replace training. The practical goal is to cheaply filter bad candidates or provide an early ranking signal.

Proxy Families

Several proxy types are commonly discussed:

SNIP

SNIP measures sensitivity of the loss to pruning weights:

The intuition is that important weights have high loss sensitivity even at initialization.

GraSP

GraSP focuses on preserving gradient flow after pruning. It uses second-order gradient information to estimate how removing weights affects training dynamics.

SynFlow

SynFlow is data-free. It propagates a synthetic signal through the network to measure path saliency and avoid layer collapse.

The figure compares zero-cost proxies on NAS-Bench-201. The useful question is not whether a proxy is perfect, but whether it is correlated enough to guide early search.

Failure Modes

Zero-cost scores are sensitive to:

  • initialization;
  • batch size;
  • normalization layers;
  • skip-connection density;
  • model size;
  • degenerate operations such as zero or identity.

A proxy may prefer larger models or architectures with better gradient flow even when they are not the best final trained models.

How I Would Use It

I would not select the final architecture using only a zero-cost proxy. I would use it as a first-stage filter:

  1. score many architectures cheaply;
  2. discard clearly bad candidates;
  3. train or surrogate-evaluate the remaining set.

Takeaway

Zero-cost proxies are useful diagnostics and filters. They are not a universal replacement for training, but they make architecture search much cheaper when used with calibration and validation.

entry.title: Real-time Federated Evolutionary Neural Architecture Search
entry.content:
Paper : Real-time Federated Evolutionary Neural Architecture Search.

I will call the method FedEvo below. The interesting part of this paper is not that it uses evolutionary NAS again, but that it tries to make NAS happen inside the normal communication loop of federated learning. A conventional evolutionary NAS setup evaluates many candidate networks after training them, while federated learning already pays a high price for every communication round. If we naively combine the two, each client would have to download, train, and upload too many models.

The paper’s answer is simple: keep one shared master model, sample sub-models from it, train those sub-models on sampled clients, and use NSGA-II to select architectures under both accuracy and FLOPs constraints.

Motivation

Federated learning has two constraints that make centralized NAS awkward.

First, clients are usually small devices. Training a whole population of candidate networks on every client is unrealistic. Second, communication is the bottleneck. Sending a full model population, or retraining every offspring from scratch, quickly dominates the cost.

The paper also points out a less obvious issue: many NAS methods rely on transfer, proxy tasks, or centralized validation. In FL, data is distributed and often non-IID, so the architecture that looks good on one data split or one client group may not be stable globally.

So the target problem is:

Requirement Why it matters in FL
Search during training Avoid an expensive offline NAS stage.
Train only small sampled models Reduce local compute and upload size.
Reuse model weights Avoid reinitializing every offspring.
Optimize model size too Edge clients care about FLOPs, not only accuracy.

Contributions

The paper has three concrete contributions.

  1. Double sampling. For every evolutionary generation, the server samples both architectures and participating clients. A client trains only one sub-model in that generation instead of a full population.
  2. Sub-model aggregation. Uploaded sub-models are reconstructed back into the master-model parameter space. Trained branches use client updates; missing branches are filled from the previous master model before aggregation.
  3. Online multi-objective search. One generation of NSGA-II is aligned with one communication round. The objectives are test error and FLOPs (the paper reports FLOPs as MACs).

The high-level loop looks like this:

The key detail is that NAS is not a separate pre-processing step. In this design, architecture search and federated training share the same rounds.

Search Space

The master network is a small CNN for CIFAR-10. It starts with a convolution block, then uses 12 choice blocks grouped by channel width: 64, 128, 256, and 512. Each choice block has four candidate branches.

Each choice block chooses one of four candidates:

  • identity block
  • residual block
  • inverted residual block
  • depthwise separable block

Because each choice block has four options, it can be encoded with 2 bits. With 12 choice blocks, an architecture choice key has 24 bits. This is a small search space by modern NAS standards, but it is enough for the paper’s point: reduce federated compute and communication while still searching over meaningful CNN blocks.

Double Sampling

The double-sampling step has two levels.

First, the server samples one sub-model from the master model according to a choice key. Instead of sending the whole supernet, the client receives a concrete path through the choice blocks.

Second, the server samples clients. If there are total clients and the client participation ratio is , then the round samples clients. These clients are split over the evolutionary population of size , so one candidate is trained by roughly clients.

This matters because each client sees only one sub-model per generation. The local workload becomes bounded by a single sampled network, not by the population size.

Aggregation

Aggregation is the part I found most useful in this paper. A client only trains the branches that exist in its sampled sub-model, but the server still needs to update one master model.

The paper handles this by reconstructing a full master-shaped model for each upload:

  • branches selected by the client use the trained client weights;
  • branches not selected by that client are copied from the previous master model;
  • reconstructed models are averaged, weighted by client data size.

This is basically weight sharing plus federated averaging, but applied at the branch level. It avoids random reinitialization of offspring models, which is one reason the real-time version is more stable than the offline evolutionary baseline in the paper.

NSGA-II Objective

FedEvo uses NSGA-II to keep a Pareto set instead of choosing one scalar reward. The two objectives are:

Objective Meaning
Test error Lower is better. Used as the accuracy-side fitness.
FLOPs (MAC) Lower is better. Used as the efficiency-side fitness.

The paper then marks two representative solutions on the Pareto front:

  • High: the solution with the highest accuracy;
  • Knee: the solution near the knee point, usually a better accuracy/FLOPs tradeoff.

One small caveat: the paper writes “test error” as the fitness. In a production FL setup, I would expect this to be a validation metric or a server-side held-out evaluation, otherwise the test set becomes part of model selection.

Experiments

The experiments are on CIFAR-10 with 50,000 training images and 10,000 test images. The paper simulates 10, 20, and 50 clients under both IID and non-IID splits. For non-IID, each client has images from 5 classes.

Important settings:

Item Value
Dataset CIFAR-10
Clients 10, 20, 50
Local epoch 1
Train batch size 50
NSGA-II population 10
Generations / rounds 500
Baseline ResNet18 for CIFAR-10
Baseline FLOPs 0.5587G MAC

The Pareto fronts after 500 rounds are shown below. Lower-left is better: lower test error and lower FLOPs.

The table in the paper is worth reading directly because it shows the tradeoff clearly.

A few rows are enough to see the pattern:

Setting ResNet18 High solution Knee solution
10 clients, IID 81.14%, 0.5587G 86.68%, 0.2796G 83.36%, 0.031G
10 clients, non-IID 80.29%, 0.5587G 81.27%, 0.2272G 78.94%, 0.0302G
20 clients, IID 82.50%, 0.5587G 85.16%, 0.2012G 83.65%, 0.0398G
20 clients, non-IID 79.91%, 0.5587G 83.01%, 0.3936G 81.58%, 0.1098G
50 clients, IID 80.78%, 0.5587G 77.10%, 0.3360G 71.46%, 0.0547G
50 clients, non-IID 77.63%, 0.5587G 75.10%, 0.1719G 69.22%, 0.0635G

For 10 and 20 clients, the best evolved model usually beats ResNet18 while using fewer FLOPs. The knee solution is more aggressive: it gives up some accuracy but cuts computation heavily. The 50-client case is weaker. The paper explains this as a data-per-client issue: when total data is fixed, more clients means less local data per client, so it becomes harder to find a stable global model.

Real-time Behavior

The real-time curves for 20 clients are the most convincing part of the experiments.

At the beginning, ResNet18 is better. That is expected: the searched models are still being optimized while the master model is changing. After about 200 communication rounds, the selected high-accuracy and knee solutions catch up and pass ResNet18 in the reported 20-client settings.

The FLOPs curves also show the point of multi-objective search. The knee solution stays far below ResNet18 in compute, while the high-accuracy solution fluctuates more because it is chasing accuracy during the search.

The paper also compares against an offline evolutionary federated NAS baseline. In that baseline, the selected model is trained from scratch for 500 communication rounds. The reported runtime is about 16.1 hours/GPU for real-time NAS over 500 generations, versus about 6.55 hours/GPU for only 50 offline generations before retraining cost. The paper summarizes this as roughly a 5x speedup per search round for the real-time method.

Takeaways

I like this paper because it treats communication rounds as the unit of NAS cost. Many NAS papers hide the search cost behind a centralized proxy task; here, the search loop is forced to live inside FL.

What I would keep from this paper:

  • Represent architectures with compact choice keys.
  • Do not ask each client to train a population.
  • Aggregate partial sub-model updates back into a shared master model.
  • Optimize compute explicitly, not as an afterthought.

What feels limited:

  • The search space is small and CNN-specific.
  • The experiments are only on CIFAR-10.
  • The 50-client results show that the method is sensitive to data fragmentation.
  • Using “test error” as the search fitness is not ideal if interpreted literally.

Overall, FedEvo is a useful early design for federated NAS: it is not the most powerful NAS method, but it gives a concrete recipe for making evolutionary search compatible with FL communication constraints.

entry.title: Hierarchical Representations for Efficient Architecture Search
entry.content:
Liu, Simonyan, Vinyals, Fernando, and Kavukcuoglu. Hierarchical Representations for Efficient Architecture Search. ICLR 2018.

Paper

This paper is a useful counterweight to early NAS papers that made the controller or optimizer look like the main story. The central claim here is simpler: if the architecture representation is well structured, even simple search methods such as random search and tournament evolution become strong.

Instead of searching one flat graph of primitive operations, the paper builds networks from motifs. Low-level motifs combine primitive operations. Higher-level motifs combine lower-level motifs. A change to a lower motif can therefore propagate through many parts of the final architecture.

Representation

Figure 1 shows the key idea. The bottom level contains primitive operations. A level-2 motif is assembled from those primitives. A level-3 motif is assembled from level-2 motifs. The final network is therefore a recursively composed graph, not just a one-shot list of edge operations.

In plain notation:

The primitive set is intentionally small:

  • 1x1 convolution;
  • 3x3 depthwise convolution;
  • 3x3 separable convolution;
  • 3x3 max pooling;
  • 3x3 average pooling;
  • identity.

The paper also uses a none operation to represent missing edges. Larger receptive fields and wider computations are meant to emerge from composing these primitives rather than adding many hand-designed primitives.

Why Hierarchy Matters

The representation encodes a strong prior: good neural networks often reuse patterns. ResNet blocks, Inception modules, MobileNet inverted residuals, and Transformer layers are all examples of repeated structure. Hierarchical NAS makes that reuse part of the search space.

The tradeoff is bias. A hierarchical representation can make search efficient when the true solution has reusable substructure. It can also hide architectures that do not fit the recursive grammar.

Representation Search bias
Flat graph flexible, but harder to search and can grow parameter count quickly
Cell-based graph reusable normal/reduction cells with a fixed macro skeleton
Hierarchical motif reusable substructures at multiple levels

This is why I read the paper as a search-space paper more than an evolution paper.

Search Algorithm

The search algorithm is asynchronous tournament evolution. A controller maintains a queue of unevaluated genotypes and a memory table of evaluated genotypes. Workers repeatedly pop genotypes, assemble the architecture, train it from scratch, evaluate validation fitness, and write the result back.

There is no ENAS-style weight sharing and no inherited weights from parent to child. Every architecture evaluation trains a model from scratch for a fixed number of steps. That makes the fitness estimate cleaner than one-shot NAS, but it also means the method still spends serious compute.

The mutation operator changes one edge in one motif:

  1. sample a non-primitive level;
  2. sample a motif at that level;
  3. sample a successor node and predecessor node;
  4. replace the edge operation with another operation from the previous level, possibly none.

This single rule can add an edge, remove an edge, or change an existing edge. In the hierarchical case, changing a lower-level motif can affect all higher-level places where that motif is reused.

Model Evaluation Setup

The paper searches for a convolutional cell on CIFAR-10, then evaluates the found cell in larger CIFAR-10 and ImageNet models.

The experimental setup has three model sizes:

  • a small CIFAR-10 model used during architecture search;
  • a larger CIFAR-10 model used for final cell evaluation;
  • an ImageNet model that transfers the searched cell to a larger-scale task.

This is similar in spirit to NASNet: search a small reusable component, then scale it. The difference is that the searched component itself is hierarchical.

Search Curves

The authors run evolution for 7000 steps using 200 GPU workers. The first 200 steps are random initialization; after that, tournament selection and mutation start.

Figure 3 has an important nuance:

  • the flat representation can reach higher small-model fitness;
  • the flat representation also tends to create larger models;
  • when the flat representation is parameter-constrained, it becomes closer to the hierarchical representation.

So the hierarchy is not magic accuracy by itself. It is a way to bias the search toward reusable structures without letting the parameter count grow as freely.

The authors also check whether search progress on the small model transfers to the final larger model. The curve is not perfectly proportional, but improvement in the small fitness generally corresponds to improvement in the large model. That matters because NAS often fails when the proxy task ranking does not transfer.

Main Results

Table 1 is the most useful result in the paper. The best hierarchical evolution run reports:

Search method CIFAR-10 error ImageNet top-1/top-5 error
Hierarchical random architecture 4.21 +/- 0.11 21.5 / 5.8
Hierarchical random search, 200 samples 4.04 +/- 0.20 20.4 / 5.3
Hierarchical random search, 7000 samples 3.91 +/- 0.15 21.0 / 5.5
Hierarchical evolution, 7000 samples 3.75 +/- 0.12 20.3 / 5.2

Two points stand out.

First, random search is surprisingly strong. With 200 samples, it is only 0.29 percentage points worse than the best hierarchical evolution result on CIFAR-10 and only 0.1 top-1 error worse on ImageNet. Because 200 samples can be evaluated in parallel, the paper reports this random-search setting as about 1 hour with 200 P100 GPUs.

Second, evolution is still the best result in the table, but the paper’s own evidence says representation quality is doing a lot of the work.

Comparison To Prior Models

On CIFAR-10, the best hierarchical evolutionary architecture reaches 3.75 +/- 0.12% error with c0 = 64, and 3.63 +/- 0.10% with c0 = 128. In the paper’s 2018 context, this is competitive with early RL-based NAS results such as NAS v3, Block-QNN, and NASNet-A.

On ImageNet, the transferred hierarchical architecture reports 20.3% top-1 error and 5.2% top-5 error. That is behind NASNet-A in the table, but still competitive with strong manual convolutional baselines from that period. The paper notes that the ImageNet model has 64M parameters, which is larger than NASNet-A’s 22.6M.

Found Cell

The learned cell uses motifs as edges. The paper notes that only motifs 1, 3, 4, and 5 are used in the final cell, with motifs 3 and 5 dominating.

The motif visualization is a good reminder that hierarchical NAS does not just learn “which operation goes on this edge.” It learns small graphs that become operations for the next level. Several motifs contain direct skip-style paths, so the final cell inherits skip connections through the motif hierarchy.

Takeaway

The strongest lesson is that search-space design can dominate optimizer design. A well-built representation makes random search a serious baseline. This paper shows that with a hierarchical motif space, even 200 random samples are competitive with a much longer evolutionary run.

The limitations are clear:

  • the method still trains candidate models from scratch;
  • the reported search uses 200 P100 workers;
  • the ImageNet model is larger than NASNet-A;
  • the hierarchical grammar is a strong prior and may exclude useful flat architectures;
  • the final result is a convolutional cell search result, not a general architecture generator.

I would use this paper as a reminder before designing a new NAS optimizer: first ask whether the representation already makes good architectures easy to sample. If random search is strong, the optimizer needs to clear a much higher bar.

entry.title: Joint Neural Architecture Search and Quantization
Large-Scale Evolution of Image Classifiers
entry.content:
Real E, Moore S, Selle A, et al. Large-Scale Evolution of Image Classifiers. ICML 2017.

Paper

This paper is one of the early large-scale demonstrations that neural architectures can be optimized by evolutionary search. It does not formulate architecture generation as a reinforcement-learning sequence model, and it does not relax the graph into differentiable operation weights. The system keeps a population of trained CNNs, repeatedly selects a parent, mutates it, trains the child, and uses validation accuracy as selection pressure.

The important point is not that one particular mutation operator is clever. The important point is that a simple, asynchronous, parallel search process can keep improving image classifiers when enough workers are available.

Search Object

Each individual is a CNN architecture plus some training hyperparameters. Mutations can change convolution filter sizes, channel counts, strides, connections, and learning-rate related settings. This is less tidy than later cell-based NAS spaces, but it is closer to the idea of evolving whole model programs.

The figure shows the best validation accuracy improving as the evolutionary process runs. The search is not just random wandering: once a good model appears, local mutations around it create a useful neighborhood for further exploration.

Tournament Selection

The loop is straightforward:

  1. Sample a small tournament set from the population.
  2. Pick the highest-validation-accuracy individual as parent.
  3. Copy and mutate it to create a child.
  4. Train the child from scratch.
  5. Insert the child back into the population and remove a weaker or older individual.

This is easy to parallelize. Each worker can train a candidate independently, then return the result. Compared with RL-based NAS, there is no controller to train; compared with differentiable NAS, there is no soft-to-discrete mismatch.

Why It Worked

Evolution is useful here because architecture quality is locally correlated. A small mutation around a good model is more likely to remain reasonable than a uniformly random sample. The population keeps multiple lineages alive, so the search is not forced into a single trajectory.

Property Practical effect
Local mutation Explores around known good designs
Population Keeps diversity and avoids one-path search
Tournament selection Adds pressure without requiring gradients
Parallel training Converts compute into exploration rate

The cost is obvious: each candidate still requires real training. This makes the paper expensive by modern benchmark standards, but it also avoids the proxy bias that later NAS systems often suffer from.

Reproduction Notes

If I were reproducing this paper, I would not only report the final CIFAR accuracy. I would first lock down three details:

  • the exact mutation space;
  • the training budget per child;
  • the asynchronous worker behavior.

The last point matters. If faster architectures return results earlier, they may enter the population sooner and receive more opportunities to mutate. That is not necessarily bad, but it is an implicit bias of the system.

I would also plot parent-child lineages. If high-performing children mostly descend from one ancestor, the search has converged. If strong models come from several lineages, population diversity is still doing real work.

Takeaway

Large-Scale Evolution is rough by today’s NAS standards: the search space is not standardized, compute is high, and the recipe is hard to compare against modern tabular benchmarks. Still, it established a durable lesson: architecture search does not have to be differentiable or controller-based. A simple black-box evolutionary system can be highly competitive when the evaluation pipeline is scalable.

entry.title: Designing Neural Network Architectures using Reinforcement Learning
entry.content:
Paper / Project / Code

MetaQNN is one of the early reinforcement-learning based NAS papers. It is worth reading together with Zoph & Le’s controller-RNN NAS paper, because the search strategy is different: instead of training an RNN controller to emit architecture strings, MetaQNN uses tabular Q-learning over a hand-designed state-action graph.

The paper is not trying to discover arbitrary neural computation. The search space is deliberately limited to standard CNN components: convolution, pooling, fully connected layers, global average pooling, and softmax. That constraint is important. The interesting part of the paper is how the authors turn “choose a CNN architecture” into a finite-horizon Markov Decision Process that can be explored with a practical amount of computation.

Motivation

CNN design contains many coupled choices: layer type, ordering, filter size, number of channels, stride, pooling position, and termination point. Exhaustively enumerating this space is impossible even when every option is discretized.

Figure 1 summarizes the whole loop: sample a topology, train it, store its validation accuracy, and update the Q-values from replay memory.

The paper’s framing is direct:

  1. Let an agent build a CNN one layer at a time.
  2. Train the sampled CNN on the target dataset.
  3. Use validation accuracy as the reward.
  4. Update the agent so that future sampled architectures become better.

This is a clean formulation, but it only works if the architecture space is constrained enough. MetaQNN therefore spends a lot of effort on the state definition and action restrictions, not only on the reinforcement learning update.

Contribution

The useful contributions are:

  1. Formulate CNN architecture generation as a finite MDP, where a trajectory is a full network topology.
  2. Define a discrete state space for common CNN layers and use action constraints to avoid invalid or obviously degenerate networks.
  3. Use Q-learning with epsilon-greedy exploration and experience replay to search the architecture graph.
  4. Show that the discovered CNNs can outperform earlier networks that use only standard convolution, pooling, and fully connected layers.
  5. Release model definitions and code, although the original implementation is tied to an old Caffe/Python 2 stack.

The last point matters historically. MetaQNN is not only a conceptual NAS paper; it includes trained topologies, Caffe prototxt files, and a server-client training setup.

Methodology

State and Action Space

The MDP view is the core modeling choice. A path through this graph corresponds to one CNN, and the green path in the figure is one sampled architecture.

Each state represents the current layer choice plus enough metadata to decide what layer can come next. The notation used in the paper is:

  • C(d, f, l): convolution with d filters, receptive field size f, and stride l.
  • P(f, l): pooling with receptive field size f and stride l.
  • FC(d): fully connected layer with d neurons.
  • GAP / SM: global average pooling or softmax termination.

The experimental search space is small enough for tabular Q-learning but still large enough to contain useful CNNs:

Layer type Main choices
Convolution layer depth < 12, filter size {1, 3, 5}, stride 1, channels {64, 128, 256, 512}
Pooling layer depth < 12, (filter, stride) in {(5, 3), (3, 2), (2, 2)}
Fully connected layer depth < 12, at most two consecutive FC layers, neurons {512, 256, 128}
Termination global average pooling or softmax

The state also includes a binned representation size. This prevents the agent from repeatedly shrinking a feature map until later convolutions or pooling operations no longer make sense. For example, too many stride-2 pooling layers can reduce a 32 x 32 image to 1 x 1, so the action graph disallows transitions that would create invalid feature maps.

This is one of the most practical pieces of the paper: NAS needs a search space, but it also needs guardrails. Without them, much of the budget would be wasted on architectures that are legal as strings but useless as CNNs.

Q-learning Loop

MetaQNN uses the standard Q-learning update:

where s_i is the current state, u is the action, s_j is the next state, and the reward r is the validation accuracy of the completed CNN. The paper sets:

  • alpha = 0.01
  • gamma = 1
  • initial Q-values to 0.5
  • final policy to epsilon = 0.1, not 0, so the final sampler can still generate several high-quality variants for ensembling

The search loop is:

  1. Sample a CNN topology by walking through the state-action graph with epsilon-greedy exploration.
  2. Train the sampled topology with a short, aggressive schedule.
  3. Store the topology and validation accuracy in replay memory.
  4. Sample 100 previous models from memory and update Q-values backward along their trajectories.
  5. Anneal epsilon and repeat.

The epsilon schedule is deliberately exploration-heavy at the beginning:

Epsilon 1.0 0.9 0.8 0.7 0.6 0.5 0.4 0.3 0.2 0.1
Unique models trained 1500 100 100 100 150 150 150 150 150 150

So one full search run trains about 2700 unique models before the final fine-tuning stage. During exploration, each model is trained for only 20 epochs with Adam, batch size 128, initial learning rate 0.001, and dropout inserted after every two layers. The reported search cost is 8-10 days per dataset on 10 NVIDIA GPUs.

Why Replay Memory Helps Here

In a normal supervised training loop, one minibatch update is cheap. In NAS, one “environment step” can mean training a CNN. MetaQNN therefore cannot afford to learn only from the most recent sampled architecture.

The replay dictionary gives each trained architecture multiple chances to update the Q-table. If the same topology is sampled again, the paper does not retrain it; it reuses the stored validation accuracy. This is a simple engineering choice, but it matters because the expensive part is CNN training, not the Q-value update.

Results

Search Behavior

The Q-learning curves are the first sanity check. As epsilon decreases, the sampled models should become better on average. The paper reports that, for SVHN, mean model accuracy increases from 52.25% at epsilon = 1.0 to 88.02% at epsilon = 0.1.

This does not prove that the agent found a globally optimal architecture. It does show that the Q-table learned useful preferences inside the constrained search graph.

The learned preferences are also interpretable. In the appendix, the authors analyze Q-values by layer depth: convolution and pooling have higher Q-values early in the network, while fully connected and termination states become more likely deeper in the network. That matches the rough shape of hand-designed CNNs.

Benchmark Numbers

MetaQNN is strongest when compared with networks using similar layer types. The top CIFAR-10 model reaches 6.92% test error, better than the standard-layer baselines listed in the paper.

Method CIFAR-10 SVHN MNIST CIFAR-100
All-CNN 7.25 - - 33.71
MetaQNN ensemble 7.32 2.06 0.32 -
MetaQNN top model 6.92 2.28 0.44 27.14
ResNet-110 6.61 - - -
ELU network 6.55 - - 24.28
Tree+Max-Avg pooling 6.05 1.69 0.31 32.37

All numbers are test error percentages. The comparison against ResNet and more complex pooling methods is less flattering, but also less direct: those models use architectural ideas outside the MetaQNN search space. The more honest reading is that MetaQNN does well within a plain CNN search space, but the search space itself limits the ceiling.

Discovered Architectures

The top CIFAR-10 architecture reported in the appendix is:

It reaches 6.92% test error with 11.18M parameters. The top five CIFAR-10 models range from 11.18M down to 1.10M parameters, but the error varies from 6.92% to 11.63%. That spread is a useful reminder: validation-guided architecture search can find good candidates, but the top architectures are not all equally strong.

One design motif mentioned in the paper is the frequent use of 1 x 1 convolution near the input. The authors interpret it as a learned linear transformation of RGB channels, similar in spirit to preprocessing into another color space. I would treat that as an observation rather than a general rule, but it is a nice example of Q-value analysis producing inspectable architecture hints.

Transfer

The authors also test whether the best CIFAR-10 architecture transfers to other datasets. SOTA means the reference state-of-the-art number listed in the paper.

Target Scratch Fine-tune SOTA
CIFAR-100 27.14 34.93 24.28
SVHN 2.48 4.00 1.69
MNIST 0.80 0.81 0.31

The architecture transfers better than the weights. Fine-tuning from CIFAR-10 weights is worse than training from scratch in all three reported cases. That is not too surprising: the searched architecture can be reusable, but the learned filters from CIFAR-10 are not necessarily a good initialization for digit datasets or CIFAR-100.

Takeaway

MetaQNN is a good example of early NAS engineering. The paper’s main lesson is not that Q-learning is the final answer for architecture search. Later work moved toward controller RNNs, cell-based search, weight sharing, differentiable NAS, and hardware-aware search because training thousands of child models is too expensive.

The lasting idea is the decomposition:

  • Define a searchable but valid architecture graph.
  • Use a cheap policy representation over that graph.
  • Evaluate sampled architectures with a consistent reward.
  • Reuse expensive evaluations through replay or other performance-estimation tricks.

The limitation is equally clear. The method inherits the bias of its search space: only standard CNN layers, coarse discrete hyperparameters, and fixed training recipes. It can discover strong combinations inside that box, but it cannot invent residual blocks, depthwise separable convolutions, attention, or hardware-aware operators unless those choices are explicitly added to the state-action graph.

For me, MetaQNN is most useful as a baseline mental model for NAS: before thinking about supernets or differentiable relaxations, first ask what the states are, which actions are legal, how much one reward costs, and whether the search space itself is the real bottleneck.

entry.title: Neural Architecture Search with Reinforcement Learning
Progressive Neural Architecture Search
entry.content:
Liu C, Zoph B, Shlens J, et al. Progressive Neural Architecture Search. ECCV 2018.

Paper

PNAS is a practical response to the cost of early NAS. Instead of generating full cells from the beginning, it grows the cell step by step. At each stage, a predictor estimates which partial cells are promising, and only a beam of candidates is expanded.

The paper is not trying to make NAS fully differentiable. It is closer to sequential model-based optimization: evaluate some candidates, train a surrogate, expand the most promising partial structures.

Progressive Cell Growth

A cell is built from blocks. Each block chooses two previous states and two operations, then combines them. PNAS starts with small cells and gradually increases the number of blocks.

The figure shows a discovered cell and how cells are stacked into full CNNs. The progressive search procedure avoids enumerating all possible full cells.

Predictor Role

The learned predictor is central. It receives a representation of a partial or complete cell and predicts its performance. The search then keeps a beam of high-scoring candidates.

This reduces cost, but it introduces predictor bias. A partial cell that is underestimated early may never be expanded. A predictor trained on early-stage candidates may also fail to extrapolate to larger cells.

Why It Works

PNAS uses the fact that architecture construction has structure. A full cell is not an atomic object; it is a sequence of design decisions. If early decisions are clearly poor, there is no need to expand them into every possible full cell.

The method is useful when:

  • full architecture evaluation is expensive;
  • partial architectures contain some predictive signal;
  • the beam is large enough to avoid premature pruning.

Results

PNAS achieved competitive CIFAR and ImageNet results with much lower search cost than early RL-based NAS. Its main contribution is not a new operation, but a more sample-efficient search procedure.

Reproduction Notes

I would check the predictor with ranking metrics, not only prediction error. NAS needs the correct ordering of candidates. A model can have low mean error while still ranking the top candidates poorly.

Beam size is also important. Too small a beam makes the method brittle; too large a beam increases cost and moves the method back toward brute force.

Takeaway

PNAS is a pragmatic NAS paper. It turns architecture search into incremental construction plus surrogate ranking. The idea still appears in modern systems: use cheap models to prune a large design space, then spend expensive evaluation only on the survivors.

entry.title: ProxylessNAS: Direct Neural Architecture Search on Target Task and Hardware
Random Search and Reproducibility for Neural Architecture Search
entry.content:
Li L, Talwalkar A. Random Search and Reproducibility for Neural Architecture Search. UAI 2020.

Paper

This paper is not trying to propose a more sophisticated NAS algorithm. Its value is methodological. It asks a blunt question: are many NAS methods really better than random search once search space, training recipe, evaluation budget, and retraining protocol are controlled?

That question is still worth asking.

Search Method vs Evaluation Method

NAS experiments mix several components:

  • search space;
  • search method;
  • evaluation method;
  • early stopping or weight sharing;
  • final retraining recipe.

The figure separates search space, search method, and evaluation method. A method may look strong because it uses a better evaluation recipe, not because the search strategy itself is better.

Random Search As A Baseline

Random search is stronger than it sounds when the search space is well designed. If many architectures in a search space are reasonable, uniform sampling can find competitive models with enough trials.

This does not mean random search is always best. It means random search is the minimum baseline. If a new NAS method cannot beat it under the same budget and recipe, the method has not shown a search contribution.

Reproducibility Protocol

A fair NAS experiment should report:

Item Why it matters
search space a good space can make any method look good
number of queries budget determines best-so-far curves
early stopping can change architecture ranking
final training recipe augmentation and epochs dominate results
seeds NAS variance is often large
released architectures enables independent retraining

Without these details, reported GPU-day comparisons are hard to interpret.

Weight Sharing Warning

Weight sharing reduces evaluation cost, but it introduces ranking bias. A child architecture may look good because it received better shared weights, not because it trains well from scratch.

The paper’s criticism is not anti-NAS. It is anti-confounding. NAS papers should isolate the contribution of the search algorithm from the contribution of the search space and evaluation pipeline.

Takeaway

Random search is the unit test for NAS. Before accepting a new search algorithm, check whether it beats random search in the same space, with the same budget, the same seeds, and the same final training recipe.

entry.title: SMASH: One-Shot Model Architecture Search through HyperNetworks
entry.content:
Brock A, Lim T, Ritchie J M, Weston N. SMASH: One-Shot Model Architecture Search through HyperNetworks. ICLR 2018.

Paper

SMASH is an early one-shot NAS method. Instead of training every candidate architecture from scratch, it trains a HyperNetwork that maps an architecture encoding to the weights of that architecture. Candidate models can then be evaluated with generated weights, which gives a much cheaper ranking signal.

This is a different path from DARTS-style weight sharing. DARTS keeps a shared supernet and selects subgraphs. SMASH explicitly generates weights conditioned on an architecture description.

Core Idea

Let (a) be an architecture encoding and (H_\phi(a)) be a HyperNetwork. SMASH uses:

to produce weights for architecture (a). The candidate network (f(x; a, W_a)) is evaluated on data without fully training (W_a) from scratch.

The target is not perfect final accuracy. The target is ranking fidelity: architectures that look good under generated weights should also tend to be good after final training.

The figure shows the memory-bank view used to encode variable network configurations. SMASH has to represent architectures in a way that the HyperNetwork can consume and turn into convolution weights.

Training Signal

The HyperNetwork is trained by sampling architectures and updating (\phi) so that the generated weights perform well. This means the HyperNetwork learns a distribution over architecture-to-weight mappings, not a separate optimizer for every architecture.

There are two important consequences:

  • the architecture encoding must preserve enough structural information;
  • the HyperNetwork capacity limits the quality of the generated weights.

If the generator is too weak, it may rank candidates by how easy they are to generate rather than by how good they are after real training.

Why It Mattered

SMASH moved NAS cost from candidate training into a reusable evaluator. That idea later appears in several forms:

Later direction Related idea
one-shot supernets amortize architecture evaluation
predictor-based NAS learn a cheap ranking model
weight-sharing NAS avoid training each child from scratch

SMASH is not the same as these methods, but it helped establish the idea that architecture evaluation can be amortized.

Limitations

The generated weights are only a proxy. A model that performs well with HyperNetwork weights may not perform equally well after full training. This gap is the central risk.

The method also becomes harder as the search space grows. Generating weights for many convolutional shapes and connectivity patterns is not cheap, and the architecture encoding may fail to capture subtle graph differences.

Takeaway

SMASH is more historically important than directly practical today. It asked a useful question: can we train one model that lets us cheaply evaluate many architectures? That question sits behind much of modern one-shot and predictor-based NAS.
